%vim its ternme contents might or might nut have been discovered by this ; even if it were he knew that the country constabulary is not a very fast-moving body and it was not arrest at Taunton that he feared, but arrest in London.

He entered a small inn and called for break- fast ; whilst it was preparing he asked for as A.B.C. railway guide. "Does this givc the trains to Minehead ? " asked the Grafter. " Yes, sir," answered the landlord, "all the trains; it's this month's guide, too. Thinking of going to Minehead, sir?" " Yes, but I don't know whether I:11 bicycle therg or not ; it all depends if my bicycle will stand the journey. burst a tyre last night and left it with a man to be mended down the street. Is Minehead a pretty place ? " Whilst the landlord was expatiating on the beauties of Minehead the breakfast was brought in and the Grafter .fell to eating with all the appetite of a man of twenty-five who has a light conscience and a good digestion. "It was a pretty shallow device," he thought, "but all the same 1 have left it j* the bucolic mind of my host that I am a cyclist on tour going to Minehead, instead of a suspected murderer making for London. 0, London 1 let me once get there and I will be free ; free as a fish swimming in the ocean, or a bird flyg in the air.' He &titled his breakfast; by the time- table he- had half an hour before the, London train started, so he did not hurry. "Is there an omnibus to the station? " he asked the red-checked damsel who presented the bill to him. "There's the London 'Hotel 'bus, sir; we can tell it to call here if you like." . .
"Hum 1" said the Grafter in a meditative voice. "I've got a bicycle 'down the street, and it's a nuisance getting it on the 'bus; no, you needn't tell it to call, I'll cycle to the station."

He walked out of the inn, smoking a cigar- ette, and at the corner of the street asked the way to the station. He thought of entering a shop to buy a cap, then he reflected that he would have to leave his straw hat behind him or carry it in his hand; to leave it behind might create suspicion, to carry it in his hand would be useless and would only draw attention to himself, and at this moment the Grafter, as far as nubile attention was concerned
They wanted it, for the red mua of West Somerset half-covered them.
" Been across the fields, sir," said the boy, as be finished one shoe.
"Yes,' said the Grafter, quite calmly as he placed the otker foot on the block. _ _

He abused himself inwardly for having been such a fool ; here was another trace left befiind him. Of course, the boy might not chance to be ouestioned. hilt it is a cardinal (11C naasmg an escape to leave as lew traces behind one as possible. His nerves were shaken by this time, or rather, they were strung up to such--a pitch that they were vibrating in •a most un- pleasant manner. He felt that he must have a stimulant of Some sort and he turned his steps to the refreshment room to obtain somo brandy.

Hole ,he was to receive a shock more stimulating than the strongest brandy could give to his system. There was only one man in the refreshment room ; he was standing with his back to the door and drinking something out of a glass.. • Jo turned as the Grafter entered, and the Grafter found himself face to face with Mr. Marcas.

It says much for the Grafter's self-posses- sion that he did not lower his eyes, or, so to speak, turn a hair; he saw at a glance that 'Alarms did not recognise him, and little er.zpcted that the muffled-up figure of, the In..d driven him and, John Stirling the night before was this young man with a pale face who had just entered the refresh- met-room and was now calling for a brandy and soda.

Marcas's manner, everything about him. spoke of a mind free from care and a confi- dene assured. He . was perfectly safe, no one had seen his face the '4lfight before ; on alighting at Lydeard he had held his hand kerchief to his mouth feigning a toothache ; he had not entered the inn, he had shuffled unknowingly the whole crime on' to the shoulders of another man.

He; like the Grafter, had slept in a barn; he had come across the country, struck the same highroad and reached Taunton about half- past seven; no one had seen him ;, he was perfectly safe, so he told himself, as he sipped his .brandy and waited for the coming of the London train.
He little knew who was standing beside ..... has- or nf the diabolical re that

a secona-class carnage, one uync.; zont other dead ; the carriage was spacterecl with blood and there were all the signs of a desper- ate struggle. One of the men was recognised as the Grafter, a notorious criminal, who had hitherto always succeeded in eluding the police the other was a man named Marcas. Marcas was dead; the Grafter had been taken to St. Mary's Hospital, where he had in the presence of the house-surgeon on duty and a police constable made a deposition declaring himself to be the sole agent in the De Morley jewel robbery. "This clears Daisy," said Miss Miggs to herself, as she folded the paper and turned homewards. "It also clears that young man, or lam very much mistaken." ' On arriving home she found baisy dressed and just about to go out. • "Daisy'," said Miss Migg," I want to speak to you ; I have something to confess." ' Confess ? "

" Yes. I have hidden something from you, but it was for your own good." She then told all. How Arthur Esmond was suspected of having robbed the London and Lancashire 'Bank, how she, Daisy, was, also suspected, how she, Miss Miggs, had thought it better to shelter her and tell her nothing of the horrible suspicion attaching to her. " Arthur suspected of robbery ? " cried Daisy in a horror-stricken voice, "of a robbery that he was not guilty of? 0, if I had only known that—if I had only known that! But how could I? The bank manager said nothing about robbery, he only showed me my own letter and asked me what I meant by a passage in it—and I ran away—what must Arthur think of me ? " , •

" I think, dear," said Miss Miggs, " that the best thing we can do at the present monient is‘ to go to St. Mary's Hospital. have a friend, a sister in the accidents ward, she will tell us all about it."

They went downstairs and Daisy .called a hansom. During the drive she scarcely spoke a word; a crowd of thoughts were facing through her brain. She had been most unjust to Arthur,. even cruel; she had bound herself to start for South Africa on Friday, and this was Wednesday; she did not even know his address; so that she would not be able to see him before she started.
The cab drew up at St. Mary's Hospital, and both ladies alighted; as they entered the building a gentleman was coming out. it %VAC Arthur Fcrrtnu,l

div.p: By H. de Vere Stacpoole.

Miss Miggs, for her greeting was cordiJ ; in fact, almost etfusive. "How fortunate," said Mrs. Bryce, when her visitor had explained the reason of her visit. "I had quite given up hope of meeting with anyone to suit me, quite, for we sail on Friday by the 'Briton.' Would the young lady be able to see me to-morrow? " "This is the young lady," said Miss Miggs, laying her hand on Daisy's arm. Mrs. Bryce was delighted; she took to the girl at once and insisted that they should both stay to dinner, to talk things over. That night when they parted everything was arranged and Daisy l had formally bound herself to be the governess of the two llitha Bryce girls and to start for South Africa loath the family on the following Friday. "I almost wish I hadn't thought of the idea," said Miss Miggs regretfully as they walked home that night, "for I don't want to lose you, that I don't. It seems to me we never meet a really nice person in this world, but we have to lose them; it's only the people who trouble us, and worry us, and bore us that stick to us. There, I'm an unzratefid oici woman to be grumbling like that instead of thanking Providence for all its mercies." Now though it sometimes happen that t person may live in London for years without meeting some other person for whom he if looking, he may meet that very same person several times running in a week. Arthur Esmond knew Daisy's address and the house and the street she lived in were for him almost sacred ground. On this evening when the lamps were lit he was walking up and down Oxford Street in the vicinity of this happy street,
Sce Daisy spoke to him in the morning his head had been in a whirl. The cruelty of her words and manner had cut deeply into his heart.

Oxford Street, that stony-hearted step- mother as Da Quincey calls it. seemed es- pecially stony-hearted to-night ; the gas lamps and the people lit by the yellow glare of the lamps seemed to Arthur like the visions one sees in a dream.

As he walked thus, s a 'farin straight before him, heedless of everything but his trouble, he passed two people in the crowd who saw him though he did not see them. They, were Daisy and her companion return- ing from Mrs. Bryce's, and the expression on his pale face went to Daisy's heart; tears filled her eyes, and a feeling of forgiveness her' mind. • turned ; had he turned too .and seen her at that moment much might have been saved that afterwards had to be endured, but he hl passed on and was already lost in the crowd. . When he returned to his rooms he found two things waiting. for him—one Was a note and the other was Mr. Struthers, porter of the London and Lancashire Lank. Struthers was one of those men who never presumed on an acquaintanceship. He had. seen Arthur in great trouble, he knew that he was under a cloud, yet his manner was perfectly respectful. The note which was awaiting him was from Estelle De Morley. It ran thus : "DEAR SIR,—I have heard of the trouble that has overtaken you owing to the loss of my father's jewels. He believes in your innocence, and so do I. I had intended calling upon you to tell you this and to see if I could be of any help, but perhaps it would be better if you were to call here and sec rw. I will be at home on the day after to-m.....;:Aa at live o'clock.
"Believe me, yours faithfully,
~ " ESTELLE DE MORLEY."
He put the letter in his pocket : .it was from a strartger, a woman, and she believed in him: Whilst Daisy, the woman who knew him, the woman who had sworn always to love him, had cast him adrift

He little knew that Daisy was ignorant of the whole affair, that she knew nothing of the accusation against him or of the suspicion against herself. Miss Miggs had never reckoned, when she decided to keep Daisy in ignorance of everything, on the fact that she was separating two lovers, perhaps for ever., Struthers had simply called to say that he hoped everything was going well with Arthur and to ask if he could be of any use. k

"I've just got my weeli''s holiday, M. Esmond," said the bank porter. "I get one every summer, and I generally go to Margate, but I'm not leaving town this time. I'll keep my eyes open, too. I know one or two, of the Scotland Yard men; detectives, not police" (Strutherg had a deep contempt for she ordinary TDoliceman), "and if I hear anything I'll keep you informed." Arthur shook him by the hand. "What a difference there is," thought he, "between the friends we know in prosperity and the friends we'find in adversity."

div.head: CHAPTER XXVII.
div.p: CHAPTER XXVII.

IT was the figure of John Stirling propped up in a corner of the carriage, dead, with a dagger in his heart and his pockets all turned inside out. The Grafter saw the whole thing atlauep. Marcas had stabbed him, robbed him, and escaped, closing the carriage door behind him. He had escaped probably at the last steep hill where they had gone at a foot pace, and where the trees over-shadowing the road had made it as dark as a cave.

Marcas must have planned the whole thing. He saw now why he had held his handkerchief to his face, why he had not entered the hotel at Lydeard, why he had induced Stirling to order a closed carriage. Then he suddenly saw his own terrible position. • He had entered the hotel at Lydeard and been recognised; he had told the landlord that tale, he had given himself completely away, and he had brought no effective disguise, for he had not intended extreme measures. Satis- fied that the two men were cowards, he had considered that the sight of his revolver would be sufficient to make them disgorge their plunder, and now he had fallen into this terrible trap. He shut the door of the carriage on its awful occupant, then he led the horse to the side of the road. Flight. That was the idea, that filled his brain. Flight, but where should he fly to? Blue Anchor was impossible; it was bounded by the sea, but it was only a small place where there were only a few fishing boats. Lydeard was impossible, for obvious reasons; the only o6urse open was to strike across the country towards Taunton and endeavour to get an early morning train to town. . . . . .

First he determined to examine the interior of the carriage and see if there were any blood- stains; if not, it might be worth while to attempt to conceal the crime by burying the body in some ditch or hiding it in some copse. He took a silver matchbox from his pocket, struck a light, and opened the carriage door. The carriage was lined with brown holland, ;and the brown holland was covered with 'bloodstains. It was useless to attempt any concealment of the body. Before he closed the door a question that had flashed across his mind was answered. How Was it that Stirling had not cried out ? A man stabbed nearly always cries out. The question was answered by a something lying upon the murdered man's shoulders; it was a loop of White cord. The sudden strangulation caused' by the pressure of a cord paralyses the rec.Arrent laryngeal nerve! and consequently the larynx ; a stifled groan, a faint gurgle is all that the victim can utter.

The Grafter knew this, and closing the door of the carriage and opening the gate of a field he led the horse and trap in. He sheltered the carriage under a group of trees, and hastily unharnessing the horse let it go free. By doing this he prevented the chance of some night policeman ineeting the trap on the road and instantly raising the hue and cry. Then he struck across the eountry in a direction, as near as he could ,reckon, to that in which-Taunton lay. As he pursued his way a rhyme came up in his head. It was the mysterious inscription on the back of the fire opal: " Who holds me tempts fate Who in darkness doth wait; To my keepers I gave The sword and the grave; The same I give thee . If my keeper thou ,be,"
CHAPTER XXVIII.

• Mtss l‘lincs after her interview with Arthut Esmond in the street returned to the house in a very perturbed state of mind. The fact that Arthur knew Daisy's address did not please her at all. He had promised to tell no one of it, but could his promise be implicitly relied on? She did not imagine for a moment that he would deliberately give information as to Daisy's whereabouts, but she knew enough about life to know that a young man in love is capable of doing very foolish things. As for Daisy, despite the scorn with which she had addressed her lover, no sooner did she find herself in her own room than she flung herself upon her bed in a passion of tears. She still loved hint. She could not escape from the fact struggle as she would. Love sometimes horribly resembles a trap from which the victim once ensnared escapes only maimed and bleeding, sometimes escapes only through death. •

So "depressed was she by the shock of such a meeting with the man she loved that she was scarcely startled when, that evening, Miss Miga9 pt.', down the sewing work she was en- gaged upon and, turning to her, said.:
- "My n dear, how would you like to go abroad? "'

" Abroad I " "Yes, I had a letter the other day from a Mrs, Bryce: she is going to South Africa and has two little daughters for whom she requires a governess. Of course, the place may be filled by this, for she starts on Friday and this is Tuesday. The governess she had engaged fell ill and that is why the notice is so short." "South Africa," said Daisy, speaking like a person in a dreani. "Yes, dear, 'South Africa, Cape Town." " I'll go," said Daisy, "if she'll take me:KI feel I will be better away from here, and then I will be able to earn my own living." "The salary is sixty pounds a year," said Miss Miggs, and ever ything found. It's not a great sum of money, but it's a competence. She is also a very nice sort of woman and I am sure you woutd like her. Shall we go round and see her, she lives in Seymour Street; an omnibus will take us there in ten minutes from here. What time is it now, seven, rather late for an ordinary visit, but thislis a visit of urgency." "But," said Daisy, "she will] want testi- monials and I have none." "My dear," said Miss Miggs, "you are my niece and that is testimonial enough for any woman. Always remember that you are my niece, not by blood relationship perhaps, but by love; a far more binding relationship than the other, let people say what they will. Well, clear, shall we go and call on Mrs. Bryce ? " Daisy assented, and twenty minutes later found them at the Mare Arch. Mrs. Bryce was at home, just going to dinner. She was a woman of about thirty-five, one of those women who have travelled far and read Tritich. Shp ouiriPntlir had q b•riaq t

div.head: CHAPTER XXIX:
div.p: CHAPTER XXIX:

As the Grafter struck across country, making, as far as he could judge, in the direc- tion of Taunton, the moon rose over the Quantock Hills, casting her light on the trees and hedges and the ghostly mist that lay upon the meadows.

_ There is something very weird in a land- scape lit by moonlight on one of those nights of summer, when the mist obscures the finer details of the scenery and ilakes wraiths of the trees and shrubs. _ _
He passed the little village of Cembe Flory and about an hour after midnight he found himself on a high road before a milestone on which was'inscribed ,

div.head: TAUNTON
div.p: TAUNTON

In a field near by he saw a ruined barn. He got over a gate and inspected the building. There -vas a cart in it, and in the cart a few sacks. He crawled into the cart and laid himself down upon the sacks. He was only four miles from Taunton, yet he Jared not go on at present; he knew that the toun,ry towns are well patrolled by the police at night, and if he were observed wandering about he might be called upon to give an account of himself. He determined to lie where he was till full daylight and then to walk boldly into the town, go to an hotel, have breakfast, and leave by the first train. He was in a desperate position, and no one knew it better than he. The whole circum- stances surrounding him were exactly like a trap set for him by Fate. The only con- solation to his wicked mind lay in the fact that Stirling had fallen also into the trap and had paid the last penalty already. The night wore away and gradually th 4 moon sunk; a rosy and seraphic dawn broke over the Brendon Hills, the sky became like a sparkling sapphire, and a song trilled upon the air. It was the sdng c' a lark which had risen from a field near by. Then the sun broke upon the landscape and %11 nature seemed to awaken, a thousand voices of birds and insects filled the air, front far-off farmyards came the crowing of cocks, voices could be heard on the road, voices of labourers going to their work; and in the distance the rumbling of a -wagon mixed itself with the other sounds.

The' Grafter felt that to delay longer might be perilous; at any moment men might come tfor the cart in which he was lying; he. got 'down, and having reconnoitred to see if any- one were near, he got over the gate and took the road to Taunton.

Four miles is not a long walk, but four miles to a man who fears arreit at every step. who stops to listen at every sound, who looks back every hundred yards to see whether he being pursued; four miles under these o& cumstances is a very long journey. At last he reached the outskirts of the town and quickened his pace, walking with a jaunty air and whistling a tune. He felt that for some hours he was fairly safe ! carriaCe

ale most selt-etfacing man in tne worla. When he got to the station there was tea minutes to wait before the train started ; bought a second-class ticket for London, in- tending to travel third. He knew quite well that if the police were after him Taunton Station would be visited, the booking-clerk would be questioned, he would pretty certainly remember having sold a second-class ticket to Paddington to a pale- faced young man in a straw hat. On the train arriving at Willesden Juiction all the second-class compartments would be watched. He would be in a third-class, and if he jumped out and mixed with the crowd there was a chance of his escaping. He walked about the platform, waiting for the train, effacing himself as much as he could by reading the notice-boards and advertise- ments.

Would the train never come in I Though nobody in particular was noticing him he felt that every eye was upon him. "The guilty flee when no man pursueth," is an axiom as true as it is old, but in the Qrafter's case, it was not the guilty who was flying but the man wh'o feared, he was suspected of guilt. There was a horrible irony in the situation. That he, who was a criminal ten times over, should now have the responsibility on his shoulders of another man's guilt seemed almost like a practical joke played upon him by that grim humourist Fate. For the first time in his career he was disconcerted. He felt that his hick had turned ; ever since he had toucht.i opal his luck had turned, he had lost heavily on some bets, he had been robbed by ,John Stirling, and now he was in this fearful position, with the gallows actually in sight. To be hanged for another man's crime, that would be the completing touch to a run of bad luck unparalleled in his experience. He felt he must do something, and a boot- black being near he determined on having his clean pd.

filled the heart of the pale young man wilo was now drinking his whisky and soda and chatting to the young lady who had served it to him. The Grafter, with his eye on Marcas and his ear strained for the- found of the 'incoming train, was rapidly arranging in his I mind his course of action. He had lost all fear for himself. To follow Marcas was the one idea that filled his brain— to follow him and have it out with him, even if he had to pursue him to the ends of the earth or the foot of the scaffold. Suddenly a hum like the drone of a huge top filled the station; it was the sound of the in-coming train. Instantly the station was astir; the sound of trucks, the clanging of milk cans, a hundred voices filled the air, mixed with the hiss of escaping steam. The refreshment room was invaded, and amidst the incoming crowd Mr. Marcas slipped out, followed by the Grafter. • A question that was exercising the latter gentleman's mind was " Will he travel first, second or third." If he travelled first it was impossible to get into the carriage with him, bearing a second-class ticket, without raising suspicions. If he travelled second it was highly dangerous to do scS for reasons before mentioned. Mr. Marcas walked along the line of carriages, looking for one in which to take his seat. Then he selected a second-cliss smoking compartment and entered it, The Grafter got in after him. For the Grafter, villain as he was, there was one thing to be said, he had at least lots of pluck. There were three people already in the compartment, two fat men, who looked like well-to-do farmers, and a thin man, who looked like a commercial traveller. CHAPTEIII XXX.

Hortnratn •tragedy at Paddington. Two men murdered. Dying man confesses to the De Morley Jewel Robbery." The news electrified London. It was on the flaming contents boards of the evening newspapers. It was being cried in the streets. Miss Miggs received it in Oxford Street. She bought a paper and hurriedly read the whoi affair. On the arrival of the early morning train from Paddinaton two men had been foun,l in

Several people had been drawn to St. Max.. Hospital by the news, Arthur amongst them. He drew back and became, pale as death when he saw Daisy. " Arthur ", cried the girl. • " Forgive me, I was ignorant, I did not know that you had been accused—Forgive me I " She took both of his hands in hers, and Miss Miggs, with the discretion of her sex in these matters, judging that it was better to leave them alone together, entered the build- ing. Going up the, flight of stone steps that leads to the main hall, the first person she saw was Lord •De Morley. He was talking to a lady who was none other than Miss Prin- ceps. They both had been drawn to the Hospital by the news. Lord De Morley, on arriving, half an hour before, had been taken to the accident ward, where, on a bed surrounded with screens, lay the Grafter. The man was obviously dying, yet when he saw De Morley he smiled. " Ah, my lord," he gasped, "we meet in a different place from where we met last. I promised you something then—" _
"The document ? '7' said De Morley. " Have you secured it ? "

screens,' he said, " better speak 10W, my lord." " I told the constable to withdraw," said De Morley," as I wished to have a word with you in private. The document." The Grafter put his hand under his pillow „...oduced a blue paper. De Morley seized it and scanned' it eagerly. Then he pat it in his pocket with a sigh of relief.

"You have acted honourably," he said. " I promised 31.,1 a large sum for this docu- ment—the money is yours." "I am dying, said the Grafter. "I want no money; you can give it to the hospitals. Dying, and all because of that opal. Since. touching it I've had no luck." "The opal—" said D e Morley. " It was smashed in the struggle in the train —I put my foot on it and ground it to pow- der. It can do no more harm—nor can I."

He turned deathly pale. "Nurse," said Lord De Morley, coming from behind ,the screen and addressing one ol the ward nurses who was close by, " yout patient seems worse." She came to the Grafter's side and lifted his hand. It. fell back inertly on the coverlet. He was dead.
CHAPTER XXXI. ENvoi A

THERE was a meeting at Miss Princaps' housu in St. John's Wood, at which were present a number of people; including Daisy Graham, Arthur Esmond, and Miss Miggs. The meeting took the pleasant form of a dinner-party.

Arthiir 'Esmond . had been cleared of all association with the jewel robbery by the Grafter's confession, so, too, had Daisy, who had not gone to South Africa ,for the very good reason that the authorities requiren her eyidence to clear Arthur. They were now engaged, and this dinner- party was a sort of betrothal feast. Miss Princeps, who sat at the head of the table, was ,a very different woman from the Miss Princeps we saw at the beginning of thi story. The agony of mind she had gon.l through had made her much more human She had assented to Daisy's marriage with Arthur, and not only assented but settled five hundred a year on. Daisy, "which," saki she, "with the two hundred a year Mr. Esmond is making at the bank is seven hundred a year, a very good income for twc young people or, at least, so they would have considered it when I was young." A relic of this story remains in the museum at Scotland Yard—the gold setting that once held the, Fire Opal, and with which though it belonged to him, Lord De Morley refused to have anything to do. The gob setting with the strange inscription: ' Who holds me tempts Fate, Who in darkness doth wait; To my keepers I gave • The sword and the grave; The same I give thee If my keeper thou be:l LTILE ENDS]

ELECTION OF OFFICERS. Councillor STOTT expressed a desire to retire from the office of secretary. His work on the Town Council and in other directions made it impossible for him to again accept the office.

-lhere were five candidates for the else of president, and the vote resulted in Mr. Plumb's re-election. Tne figures were Mr. Plumb, 15 ,• Mr. J. Podmore, 5 ; Mr. E. Plinston, 5; Mr. Greeley, 4, and Mr. W. H. Rifillardson, 0. A like number of candidates were nominated for the vice-presidency, and the first vote resulted as follows :—Mr. F. S. Massey, 8 ; Mr. J. Greeley, 8 ; Mr. W. Healey, 6 ; Mr. E. Plinston, 6 • and Mr. A. Graham, 0. A second vote resulted in the election of Mr. Massey who received 15 votes as against 14 given on behalf of Mr. Greeley. Mr. E. Plinston was a strong candidate for the position of secretary and was returned by 17 votes, the other nominees receiving—Mr. W. Hickinbottom, 9 ; and Mr. J. Corrin, 3. Mr. T. Howliston was re-elected treasurer without opposition as were also Messrs Corrin and Plumb, delegates to the Labour Representation Com- mittee. Ont of eleven candidates Messrs. Corrin J. Haley, Hickinbottom, and J. Podmore and Councillor Stott were elected to constitute the Exectutive Com- mittee. The retiring members were Messrs. J. Edge, Bickinbottom, Plinston and Podmore. Councillor STOTT reported that all returns to the questions regarding the unification Of labour had not been made.

It was decided to adjourn the question for a month and to call for the returns to he made in time for the next meeting of the Council. • THE "BEAMONT" SCHOOL. PAYMENT OF LABOTJRERS. Councillor STOTT gave a lengthy statement in explana- tion of his action with regard to the payment of brick- layers' labourers in connection with the " Bearnont " Council school. He felt that in paying sd. an hour to men who by mechanical means supplied the bricklayers with material, the contractor was committing a breach of the standing orders of the Corporation. He (Coun- cillor Stott) maintained that the men who supplied the bricklayers whether by the hod or by any other means were labourers and were entitled to 6d. an hour. The contractor, and the Master Builders' Federation who backed him up, believed that there was no breach of the standing orders as the men were not bricklayers' labourers, but he (Councillor Stott) would like to point out that other builders in the town paid men similarly employed ad. per hour as labourers. He was firmly con- vinced that the contractor was wronc and intended to raise the question at the next meeting of the Council. It was resolved "That this Council endorse the action of Councillor Stott and Mr. E. Plinston and protests against the Education Committee allowing Jr. Davenport to continue the contract under the condi- tions reported, and calls upon the Town Council to refuse to confirm the action of the Education Com- mittee."

Councillor STOTT explained that it was proposed that school fees should be charged in the " Beamont " school. He intended to protest against this if and it were approved he would suggest that they should send a petition to the Board of Education. (Elear. hear.) A vote of thanks to Councillor Stott for his services as secretary concluded the meeting.

--- LECTURE BY Mn. CAMERON, m.p.—The members of the Penketh Wesley Guild were favoured by a visit from Mr. R. Cameron, M.P., on Wednesday evening. Mr. Dodds should have given a paper on his visit to Waterloo, but on proVding such a splendid substitute be was excused for the time being, and given a cordial greeting as chairman for the veteran M.P. Mr. Cameron delivered a magnificent lecture on "Books, and bokv to read them." He held a large audience entranced for over an hour by the beauty of his thought and language, combined with rare insight and know- ledge. While the lecture was an inspiration it was also' a revelation to most of how casually theyhave traversed the field of literature. Mr. Cameron advised all to cultivate a passion for reading the best 'books of all ages.—At the closet the Rev. E. J. Gawne conveyed the warm thanks af the Guild members and friends to both Lecturer and Chairman for the great and unexpected treat which had been afforded.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRADES COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TRADES COUNCIL.
ANNUAL MEETING. Contest for Official Positions

The annual meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council was held in the Wesleyan Schools, Bold- street, on Tuesday evening, Mr. T. Plumb presiding over a good attendance of delegates. At the outset it was decided to endorse the candida- ture of Mr. Pook, I.L.P.nominee in Orford Ward.

div.head: SECRETARY'S REPORT.
div.p: SECRETARY'S REPORT.

Councillor STorT, in presenting the t ist annual report, said that the Council commenced the year with an increase in the number of branchesalilliated, but with a slight decrease in the total membership as represented through the branches. It was hoped that during the coming year the extending of the work of the Council would encourage other societies to join, and that the Council might become representative of the whole of the trade union forces in the town. where had not been any, trade dispute of any importance during the year -a fact which was as pleasing to them as to ar.ty section of the community. Although there had been a general improvement in trade the building industry had suffered from lack of employment as evidenced by the large number reported as unemployed month by month. The present time appeared favour- able for securing improved conditions for those engaged in the metal trades. The Government had not however dealt with the QUESTION OF THE INEMPLOYED

in a manner which was to be expected,juiiin-g from their pre-election sposeches and having regard to the gravity of the question. Their grant of £200,000 was quite inadequate for the %requirements of the unemployed. The Council had ',assisted in the formation of the Right to Work Committee in Warrington. He trusted that they would continue to support the movement to secure more generous and sympathetic consideration of the claims of those who were out of work. Since the passing of the last Unemployed Act a Distress Cnmmittee had been formed in Warrington but owing to the limited powers it bad done little beyond opening an unemployed bureau. In Mr. Fargher they had an excellent servant and a friend of the unemployed and who bad been the means of securing work for many who would not otherwise have obtained it. Last year be (Councillor Stott) tried to persuade the Town Council to adopt a minimum wage of 245. per week for all able-bodied Corporation employees arid though he was not successful the Corporation subsequently adopted a minimum wage of 21s. He trusted that in the near future they. would be able to have the wage increased to a sum sufficient to emable a man and his family to live in decency and comfort. They had been interested in the experiment made by the Council during the past year in having the markets painted by direct labour. , That experiment, had, he was pleased to say, proved quite successful. The work had been better done than by contract and from a financial standpoint the venture was also successful. The Trades Council had, however, I , bad to protest against such a large number f non-nnion 1 painters beillg engaged on the work. That was a grlev- , ance which could only be remedied by them securing the return of a sufficient number of labour members to the I Town Council. He would like to see the principle of direct employment extended to other Corporation departments, believing that, it would tern the best interests not only of the trade unionists of the town, but of the ratepayers. Councillor Stott proceeded to refer • to National Administration. He believed that they could shortly expect a satisfactory Trade Disputes Bill to pass the House of COMMODS but no Bill would be satisfactory which placed their organ- isations and accumulated funds at the mercy of unscrupulous employers who thought they could make a legalized raid upon them.ln regard to the Trade Disputes Bill he thought they werejustified in the protest against the absence fr3m the division of the Member for War- rington. Numerous improvements had been made in committee to the Government Compensation Amend- ment Bill. What was desired was a Bill which would give compensation for injuries to all workers and in order that the compensation should be guaranteed it was desirable that a national scheme of compulsory insurance should be set up. (Hear, hear.) Questions of old-age pensions, payment of members and election expenses, the feeding of necessitous children &c., had met with the ,sympathy of the government who, how- ever, pleaded that the money could not be found to carry the measures into operation. He thought that the labour members would he able to show the Government how the necessary sums could Fe provided. The Council still retained its membership of the Labour Representation Committee but had to regret that owing to lack of support the work of the Committee had not been very great. It was a matter for regret that after two years useful work on behalf of labour, Councillor ' Wright, owing to continued and serious ill-health, might be prevented from seeking re-election. Councillor Stott on behalf of the Council proceeded to tender thanks to Councillors Wright and Ball and to Mr. E. Plinston for their whrk On behalf of labour. One of the most important questions which they had raised during the year was the UNIFICATION OF LABOUR FORCES • in Warrington. It had been felt for some time that there wee too much overlappiug by having so many labour organizations but unfortunately at a conference of labour 'bodies which was held, whilst the principle was heartily endorsed they were enable to agree as to the constitution of the central authority. The Council, anxious to avoid friction which would weaken their forces, had addressed a list of questions to the branches, the result of which, he trusted, would be the formation of one organization to congider matters /affecting trade unions and also to take their part in the political life of the•town. In their opinion such an organization would be able to weild an influence in the town which had hitherto not been attained by the labour movement/ (Applause.) ,

Madame Patti's Farewell.—Madame Adelina Patti's concert at the Royal Albert Hall on December Ist will, it is announced, be her last in London, and next year she will bring her professional career finally to a close. It has been a remarkably successfulcareer, and no singer of her own or any other time has approached Adelina ' Patti in the fabulous sums she has earned by her wonderful voice. Born of Spanish parentage in 1843, she was an" infant prodigy "in 1850, when she sang for the first time in public. The next eight years were devoted to study, and at fifteen she appeared in New York in the role of Lucia, when her success was instan- taneous. That established her reputation as a singer of the highest rank, and in 1861 she took London by storm, in the part of Amine, in ha Sonnambula, and for many years afterwards she sang regularly at Covent Garden. Madame Patti has been thrice married, lastly in 1899 to Baron Cederstrom, of Sweden, but who is now a natural- ised British subject. Seventy Years Married.—lt is so rare an event for people to be able to celebrate the seventieth anniversary of their wedding, that it is said there is only one older married couple in the United Kingdom than Mr. and Mrs. John Brinsmead, who were married on June 3rd, 1837. That is doubtless an under estimate and in all probability investigation would show that there are other couples living who can look back upon seventy years of married life, but in any case it is not given to imany to live, like Darby and Joan, so long in the land. Mr. John Brinsmead is in his ninety-third year, and founded the famous firm of piano manufacturers in 1837, the same year in which he was married. Both he and Mrs. Brinsmead are hale and hearty, and iNfr. Brins- mead still attends to the business which he has so long and successfully conducted. The Careless Clubwoman.—Although women's clubs have long become a recognised feature of social life,yet sarcastic remarks are occasionally still made about the clubwoman. The carelessness with which she leaves her possessions about, has caused some of the principal women's clubs to establish a regular " Lost and Found Property " office, and so great is the reputation of the clubwoman, for losing things, that the Police furnish some of the clubs with a list of articles found in cabs, in expectation that the owner may be known therein. The lists on the clubs" Lost and Found " notice boards always includes umbrellas, fans, feather boas, bracelets, purses, jewellery of all kinds, canes, cigarette cases parcels, and in fact everything from is pocket handker- chief to a sable coat, which a woman could possibly leave behind. What is even more astonishing is, that many of the aiticles " found "are naver claimed, the owner apparently waiting for the club to hold a bargain sale, when perhaps she will buy back her own things with the keenest possible interest. _ _NtVomen and Club Life.—Leigh Hunt, writing nearly y yea.rs ago, and predicting the advent of women's e übs, chd not believe that they„would hare an ,advers4 influence upon domestic life. • Those women,' he said if' who were comfortable at home, would like their own houses the better for the variety, and those who were not had better, for the sake of all parties be elsewhere." Hs was thinking, of course, of those who had the makings of a comfortable home but there are many people who, although comparatively well-to-do lead lonely lives in the great cities and for such as these the Rev. W. J. Cornersall has started. "The Eligible and Social Circle " Club in London, open to men and women. This is a much less formal affair than the usual club, and is intended to provide various entertain- ments and social evenings for its members. Harris Tweed.—The London tailor who has come to grief through selling factory cloth as Harris tweed, will have done, 'without any credit to himself, a great deal of good for that remote cottage industry. It is true that his sentence of imprisonment has been reduced to a heavy fine, but that will be sufficient to sheck the fraud of supplying an inferior manufacture as genuine Harris tweed, of which the Duchess of Sutherland and others who have the cottagers' interests at heart, have so often complained. No one did more for the industry than the late Dowager Countess of Dunmore, and it was largely due to her encouragement that Harris tweed acquired the excellent repultition that it possesses. Her son, the present Earl of Dunmore owns the greater part of flarris Island, and continues, as far as possible, the excellent work accomplished by his mother in pro- moting hand-loom weaving amongst the cottagers. Evening Wraps.—With the help of a good pattern, so easily obtainable now-a-days, the fashioning of an even- ing wrap should present few difficulties. One of the simplest and easiest styles, perhaps, is the " burnous," so called because of its close similarity to an Arab's cloak. The long sweeping folds are generally most becoming, moreover there is no possibility of such a wrap crushing the gown beneath. For walking par- poses, or travelling to and from the suburbs by theatre trains, however, the loose three-quarter coats are cosiest and best. The sleeves should be big and roomy, drawn into wide cuffs at the wrist, and a hood, amply large, and very light in weight, is a very necessary addition. Cashmere or cloth, are ideal fabrics for such wraps, which should be lined with silk or satin, or a "silky mixture," and have an interlining of flannel or flannel- ette. Some of the dainty white furs, now being offered at such moderate figures, would make a soft and becoming finish to the collar and cuffs. New Sleeves.—The " trimmed " sleeve is "in " again, and to all save those who are too "generously covered," the notion will be a Welcome one. The sleeve that is made up of a series of puffs from shoulder to wrist is in high favour, and is quite a change from the " bag" below, or above the elbow which we have had with us so long. Then we have the tucked, gathered, and piped sleeves, and the sleeve covered entirely with frills. The sleeve ending at the elbow is not seen at the leading tailors, and only very dressy day toilettes are built with the elbow sleeve now. This Is an item for which we should be thankful. Our arms-Thom waist to elbow—are not our strong point, RS we have had ample opportunity for assuring ourselves, during the past few months, and they would be all too likely to prove even less fascinating when the cold winds of winter had played further havoc :with them. Ornamental Het Pins.—Hat pins—or rather the beads thereof—are of such huge dimensions, that they form part of the trimming of the hats they are used upon. The velvet flower hat pin is having a great vogue, and milliners are making a point of providing pins that match each set of floral trimming.—Then there ate the enormous mother-of-pearl, and crystal balls, so modish just now, and a decided novelty is the huge fiat disc, covered with tartan velvet. "I did not think of the grave risk that one runs by neglecting a chill, and that is how the mischief started in my case," said Mrs. Rose Proctor, of 9, Leopold-st., Claremont, Halifax, to a reporter. "Yet I have to thank Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People that I am so strong and well to-day. I thought little of the chill at first, and was hoaxed into leaving it to mend itself. But very quickly it settled on me; I lost colour and fell away as if I were starving. Indeed, in a few weeks I really was starving, because I could not eat anything at all on account of the inflammation of my throat and the pains which attacked me in my chest after forcing down a mouthful of food. Every morn- ing I felt dazed and weary, and wanted to sleep longer.

MY HEAD FELT AS NEAVY AS LEAD; - and sore from constant pain. I was continually shivering though the day might have been quite mild. I lost all sense of taste and smell, and at last could only obtain fitful unrefreshing sleep. Then a heavy, gnawing pain settled across my shoulders and down my back, which seerdied to lose all strength; my knees pained me dreadfully. The exertion of going up a few stairs thoroughly tired me and left me gasping. "When I fully realised that I was going down hill rapidly I fought hard to keep my spirits up and regain my health. [feared that I might follow others whom I had watched grow pale and breathless, and then sink rapidly and die. So I went under the best medical treatment for months, but lost hope in everything, for I spent pounds on advice and medicine. Physic proved worthless to me. THE FREE CHURCHES AND SOCIAL QUESIONS. One of the results of the increasing attention devoted to social work by the Free Churches is the publication early next month of a volume entitled " The social mission of the Church." The book is intended to be an exposition of Free Church opinion on this important subject. At the request of the Social Questions' Com- mittee of the National Free Church Council, the Rev. C. Ensor Walters has kindly edited, the volume. The con- tributors include such eminent Free Church leaders as :—Revs. J. Scott Lidgett, F. B. Ateyer, Dr. Clifford, Dr. Horton, Dr. Brook, Dr. Townsend, Dr. Gibson, R.g J. Campbell, Professor Peake, &c. The volume will be published by the National Free Church Council.

THREE MONTHS WASTED. A postcard of the usual size is exhibited at the Bucharest Exhibition. On it is written the Bulgarian Constitution in full, the opening speeches of various European Parliaments and two poems by Rurlyard Kipling-12,000 words in all. Peter Paikoo, of Sofia, spent nine hours a day for three months to accomplish the feat.

div.head: WARRINGTON EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRINGTON EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
TEACHERS' REPORTS.
Question of Abolishing School Fees.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Education Committee was held at the Town Hall ou Monday when there were present : Aldermen Bennett (presiding), Evans, and Smethurst, Councillors Fulton Smith, Pemberton, Lord, Ellison, .7. Evans, Sankey, Ball and Barton, Miss Williams, Revs. Canon Morley Stevenson, and J. Davies and Messrs. H. Roberts, H. Kingdon, E, Plinston, A.. 1. Jolley, G. Walker, C. H. Unsworth, J. Upson, C. E. Parker, and J. Moore Murray (director of education.)
QUESTION OF SCHOOL FEES. TIME NOT OPPORTUNE FOR ABOLITION.

In moving the adoption of the minutes of the Finance Committee Mr. A. J. JOLLEY referred to the decision of the committee to chitrge school fees at the " Beamont " Council schonl. So long as fees were charged in the other schools it was, be ventured to suggest, desirable that they should be charged in the schools which the committee provided. Any argument which could be brought forward for the relieving of the I provided schools P was really an argument against fees I being charged at all in the town. To abolish the fees in the new schools would be to set up an unfair com- petition which would seriously cripple some of the other schools. The total abolitton of fees meant an increase in the rates of 3d. in the £. Councillor SANKIIY seconded.

Councillor BALL said he objected very strongly to the resolution of the committee. the argument appeared to be that if no fees were charged in the new school they would have to be abolished in all schools or it would interfere with the work of the so-called voluntary schools. He did not need to enter into an argument about school fees in general but be thought that they should provide accommodation and education for school children without charge. He did not see that the abolition of fees would mean an increase of 3d. in the £, but even then an education rate should be levied for oeducation purposes so that they would know the entire coat to the community. He thought there should be no barrier whatever against even the pooreSt and meanest child having the fullest and best facilities for education which they could offer. He moved that the minute be not confirmed.

Mr. PLINSTON seconded and referred to the proposal by the committee to provide 90 free places in each department of the school. That was doing something to which he was very strongly opposed. It was a very difficult thing to give free places when the me lium through which parents had to proceed to take advantage of them marked them out as paupers. If they were going to"charge fees they should charge all cuildren and if they were to have a system of pauperism the parents could apply, through the existing medium for relief. He thought ita move in the wrong direction and that the school should be entirely free. Mr. ROBERTS said that whilst largely in favour of the spirit of the amendment he did not think it was a practicable proposition at the present time. Unless the committee was prepared to discuss the whole question of freeing the schools and to settle it as a question of principle to be applied to the whole of the schools, he thought the difficulty and invidiousness to which Mr. Plinston referred in making free places would be intensely increased by making a free school. If they had a free school how were they going to select the children which should attend it? Were they to accept the that comers or to consider the financial posi6ions of the parents ? At the proper time he was quite prepared to look favourably upon adding the whole of the cost of education to the rates of the town but until they were prepared to free the schools entirely they had no right to add to the difficulties of administration by making one school free to the very great disadvantage of all the other schools and to the possible advantage of many parents who did not need assistance. Mr. JOLLEY said the abolition of school fees in town would unquestionably mean an addition of 2d. in the £ to the rates, and in not more than twelve months of at least another penny. With regard to Mr. Ball's plea for the poorest child, he would point out that there was now no barrier, as free places were provided in every school in the town. Since its formation the Committee had been trying to construct an educational ladder, not merely in respect to the elementary school, but with higher education, with the result that the poorest child which showed a capacity to profit by higber education could get the full benefit of even the universities. On a vote being taken only Councillor Ball, Mr. E. Plinston, and Mr. G. Walker voted for the amendment. The minutes were approved. TEACHERS' REPORTS.

In regard to the question of periodical reports upon teachers' work the School Management Committee resolved, that in future, the reports upon the conduct and work of the assistant teachers be only required from the head teachers and managers when the same are of an unsatisfactory character ; and that, when such a report is received, the teacher so reported upon shall be notified of the fact, and shall be afforded an oppor- tunity of stating his or her case before the Committee. The Rev. Canon STEVESNON in moving the adoption of the minute pointed out that the recommendation was the same as the One which the Education Com- mittee refused to confirm at its previous meeting. The sub-committee had very carefully re-considered the matter and were convinced that no great good would come from making any alteration in the resolution and thought that the desired object would be achieved by getting reports upon teachers whose work happened to be unsatisfactory. He did not see.why the head teachers should be burdened by adding largelo to their work by calling for a report upon the work of the whole of the assistant teachers. He would assure them that the sub- committee had not treated the committee in any cavalier spirit but had most carefully and thoroughly considered the matter. They would see that the Board of 11:duca- tion had written pointing out the need for additional accommodation at the secondary school and that a con- erence had been arranged between the committee and representatives of the Board. The Committee could take the letter from the Board as an indication that they intended to ask for further accommodation. Councillor_FULTON SMITH seconded. .

Mr. A. J. JOLLEY moved that the recommendation with regard to teachers' reports be not approved. To put it mildly he did not think that the attempt which lay behind the resolution should be allowed to succeed. The resolution which, in effect, it was proposed to rescind, was a definite instruction from the Education Committee, and called upon head teachers to supply half-yearly reports upon the conduct and work of the assistant teachers. When the Committee came into existence adequate provision was made for a scale of salaries by which teachers were to getannual increments up to a reasonable maximum. He ventured to assert that it was their very strong opinion that those increments should not be merely automatic, but should be in recognition of faithful and satisfactory service. He submitted that it would be a failure of duty on the party of any authority to allow a scheme so designed to become automatic and to allow the inefficient to benefit as much as the diligent teacher. (Hear, hear.) The resolution of the sub-committee seemed to be putting a premium on inefficiency. It was impossible for them to do their duty in applying the scale unless they received from competent persons reports upon the work of those who would benefit under the operation of the scale. He did not suggest that the original resolution was satisfactory. In his opinion it was not sufficiently strong but it was a slight safeguard. There was the objection to it that it imposed additional work upon the head teachers. As one who knew a little about the working of the schools he ventured to say that such an argument was simply and supremely silly. There were plenty of men in business who had to work harder than the head teachers who did not grumble if they had a little extra work put upon them land he objected to the suggestion that the original resolution was intended to overburden the head teachers.

Mr. ROBERTS seconded the amendment. The question was as to whether a reasonable instruction giveleby the revonsible authority was to be complied with or not. Even if .the original proposition was not reason- able they had a right to ask of their stall that it should be complied with. The Chairman of the committee asked that they should not put an additional burden upon the head teachers. If ever there was a bit of special pleading with which he had had to deal it was that. In the report for which they asked there were five columns to be filled in. In the first was to be placed the name of the assistant teacher, second observations as to punctuality, third character and conduct, fourth efficiency as a teacher ; and fifth, and he thought this was a most efficient safeguard to the assistant teacher, the managers' com- ments on the head master's report. That in itself was a guarantee against any improper use of power by a head teacher who was prejudiced against one of his assistants. Proceeding Mr. Roberts said that when the original instructions of the committee were issued a certain head teacher of thetown went to three assistants and said to them" Look here, you will have to hustle or I shall have to report adversely upon your conduct." llf proof were required of the necessity of systematic Chapter 7

div.p: AGED 100, AND STILL PREACHING.

Though 100 years old, the Rev. Thomas L. Lord, of Horncastle, was able to preach on Sunday night to a large congregation at liusliden, where every word of his sermon was audible, and his lesson nos a chapter quoted from memory. He referred to a previous visit to the town, some 70 years ago, and expressed his pleasure at seeing the descendants of many old friends.

Mr: COCKERTON, the Local

_ THE CHURCH Government Board auditor, AND THE BIBLE, has a way of becoming vastly important now and again. A few years since his name became known throughout all England because he refused to sanction certain expenditure on the higher kind of education which was being provided by the London School Board. He is now auditing the accounts of the London County Council, and two deputations, each with a different object,hut really urging the same point,have asked him to deter - mine the true inwardness of the West Riding judg - merit just as if he were in a position to declare, in difficult circumstances like the present, what is the actual law of the land. If Mr. COCKERTON does not feel more self-important than ever Government auditor did before he must have great strength of character or phenomenal modesty. But more important for the moment even than Mr. CocKErtrox were some of the things that were said to him. F r example, Canon BitooKs, speak- ing for the National Society for educating children in the Religion of the Church of England,said that if any surcharge was made in respect of denomina • tional teaching he and his friends would demand that a similar surcharge should be made in regard to simple Bible teaching. This is an empty threat, of course. The West Riding judgment does not affect such teaching as is given in schools that are under public control. What Canon' BROOKE said is, nevertheless, of much significance. It is an expression of the attitude of large numbers of —Churchmen, we were going to say; but let us substitute ecclesiastical and clerical per- sons, towards the Bible. They frankly treat it as a dangerous book. The Bishop of London says, without mincing his words, that Church schools were built to avoid simple Biblical instruction. He is right, no doubt, in regard to the numerous Church schools erected after the passing of the Education Act of 1870. They were intended to prevent the intrusion of the School Board, and to give the Church, in rural districts at least, complete control over the educa-

tion of the young. But nobody at that date would have stated their object in the words now employed by Bishop INGRAM. Outside the Roman Catholic Church there can have been hardly any- body who regarded simple Bible teaching as some- thing evil and dangerous. The central position of CITILLINGWORTIeS " The Religion of Protestants," a book which at one time had a great deal to do with the moulding of the religious feeling of England, is that the religion of Protestants was the open Bible. Had he been told that a day would come when Protestantism would be spoken of by Churchmen as a thing abhorred, and when simple Bible teaching would be regarded by some Bishops and some Canons as a danger to religion, he would have declined to believe in the possibility of any such thing Apprehension lest the Bible should do harm if not accompanied by dogmatic teaching is a new thing among English Churchmen. It is none the less real, however, and it is well that the fact should be known, for which reason we are grateful to the BIsHoP oF LoNnorr nd others for stating it with so little.circumlocu- tion. The objection to simple Bible teaching, on the part of such dignitaries of the Church as Bishop INGRAM and Canon BRooRR, will clear the way for what is the final and inevitable solution of the Education question. If the Bishops, if bodies like the National Society, object to simple Scripture instruction, if they would rather have no reading of the Bible at all than the reading of the Bible without doctrinal comment, we ought not to be far from the day when the schools maintained by the State will teach only what is important to the ;life of the citizen, and when the teaching of religion will not be the business of the schoolmaster but of the home and of the Churches. Opposition to simple Bible teaching is, in fact, driving us rapidly towards the secular solution of the Education question, and,for that reason,whilst we disapprove we cannot wholly condemn it.

Mr. Havelock Wilson, M.P., ME. HAVELOCK the eloquent and hard- WILSON, M.P. working seamen's repre- sentative, was strong in his criticism of the Independent Labour party at Warrington on Thursday. He issued a unique challenge to this effect : That if all the Indepen- dent Labour Party men were got together from all ends of the country, ho could prove that he had done more fighting for Labour in one year than the whole lot of them bad done in a life-time. He emphasized the fact—and wisely too--that the action of the Shipping Federation was an attack on Trade Unionism. This is sn obvious that we wonder more and more at the Trades and Lsbour Council's " masterly inactivity" when they should have been in the forefront defending such a champion of their interests as Mr. Wilson. The supineness of the Coancil was farther condemned by Mr. S. Wright,J.P.,one of its ex-presidents,and the work- ingmen generally will,we should think, be anxious to dissociate themselves from such an unaccount- able course of action as the Council has adopted.

Until after the November THE MAYORALTY. elections the question of the Mayoralty remains in abey- ance, but there is none the less interest taken in it at the present moment. Public opinion that a change is necessary in the holder of the office is, we believe, unanimous. Alderman Bolton has filled the position for three years now, and has earned a considerable amount of public gratitude for his strict attention to corporate business. But no one could °contend with justice that he has been an ideal Mayor. He has failed—and we do not say it unkindly—in one essential particular, i. e. as chairman of the Council. There was never a time in the history of the Borough when a firm, impartial chairman was so absolutely necessary as at present. The Council contains a large proportion of men who are comparatively new to public office and they do not always conduct themselves as they should in debate. We hasten to add that they are / not alone in possessing this fault. Some of the older members are frequently responsible for interruption and disorder. Time is wasted and patience w threadbare at nearly every meeting or the want of a firm, guiding hand. There is only one member of the Council whom we think is really well qualified and adapted for the position which will soon be vacant, and the g,entleman in question rs Alderman l'ierpoint. He is one of the oldest members, has never been Mayor, and o u n i osny s o that htaht e hliaarg ree tmajorityur,, would of alltit more than one previous occasion ho has been pressed to accept the office. The position again for opinions a awaits his acceptance, and we are convinced that wei partiesood ir witcwcee ohhe tilfe p n v igne Alderman Pierpoint possesses the ad ht character and tact so necessary at tho hailed present moment, and we sincerely hope he will not again disappoint his native town by declining to become its Mayor.
The teachers have WM a TEACHERS' REPowrs. notable,.if bloodless victory . .

this week. A certain section of the members of the Education Committee wished to over-ride the School Management Committee on the question of teacher's reports and make it compulsory for head-masters to report half-yearly on the conduct and efficiency of their staffs. All that the school-management Committee recommended was that reports should be required from head-masters and managers only when they were of ail unsatisfactory character, and in that case the teacher implicated by the report was to have the opportunity of appearing in self-defence before the Committee. Resolu- tions to this effect came up for confirma- tion on Monday for the second tune, the committee being unshaken in its views, and not- withstanding an amendment the resolutions were eventually confirmed. The Education authority has an employer's right to insist on receiving a report when there is anything to complain of, but it would have been unwise and unnecessary to arbitrarily demand that every teacher should be reported upon twice a year. Teachers belong to a class of responsible public servants and their res- ponsibility is not only to the Education Committee, hut to their headmasters, who can surely be trusted with the management of their own department. They themselves are as much interested in securing efficiency and good conduct as the most ardent educationist who may have been appointed to serve on the central authority, and an implicit trust should be placed in them. A too inquisitorial attitude on the part of the Education Committee would conduce neither to the smoothest working of the educational system nor to the best grounding of the young in the three R's.

Why is it that in Franca THE TRAMP and Germany there are no PEsT. tramps whilst the rural parts of Great Britain are overrun by them? To say that such vagabonds are discharged soldiers is a wicked libel on those men who have worn the King's uniform and have had the virtues of cleanliness and discipline drilled into them. Unfortunately, the most nomadic hymen beings, who for centuries were always ihifting their abode, were the troubadours, the linnesingers, or the wandering minstrels. These ialuded not a few exceedingly clover men of great Atical abilty. In consequence they were welcomed not merely by the poor but by the proudest aristoc- racy, for they had the talent to entertain the lord, and especially his lady. It was these men who ;lairned that a vagrant was everywhere at home, that the true vagabond was the only king lye all comparison. Such ideas, handed down poet to poet, and incorporated in some of our ~ verse, have surrounded the tramp of to-day ith a peculiar glamour, so that, although it is !tierally admitted that he is an unmitigated lisance, he is secretly encouraged by women with isceptible feelings, who regard his uncleanliness id disgraceful garments as a mere disguise the latent romance which they conceal. the professional vagrant thrives; and begs, Jorrows, or steals, to the disadvantage of the genuine unfortunate, whose life is one long-con. *wed apology through no fault of his own. ct-`41.15, owing to our topsy-turvey system of helping F 107 wrong people, philanthropists support every. ?ere vagrants who are sufficiently artful to de- c Env' !) whilst the charitable unwittingly neglect and \ rshdeeper into the mire those who would benefit . ce state if a helping hand were held out to them tie right moment. In these degenerate times !ne most unpoetical person is the tramp. He can even sing a good song in return for a piece of per. The best proof that he is not a former 'eldier is that in the two greatest military nations Ipulsory service has eliminated the vagrant.

' Spiritualist Anniversary. The anniversary services in connection with the Warrington Spiritualist Society were held on Sunday. An open session was held in the afternoon, whijh was fairly. well attended by adult members of the congregation. Mrs. Jessie Greenwood, of Hebden Bridge, a prominent worker in the Lyceum movement, gave an interesting address to the Lyceum, and recitations were given by some of the scholars/ In the evening the hall was crowded, the platform being filled with scholars, who sang a number of Lyceum songs. Mrs. Greenwood was the speaker, and after performing the ceremony of "naming "a baby in a most impressive manner, gave an 'address on the importance of the right training of children, intimating that its results would be more manifest in the next generation, for so much depended upon the character of the parents. The address was listened to with the closest attention. Mr. Joel Foster presided efficiently at the organ. On Monday evening a public tea was held, followed by a socisl, at which Mr. F. Monks and Mr. Joseph Foster presided at the piano. TABLE FLOOR, AND HANGING LAMPS in large variety. 'Latest patterns.—J. S. GARLAND, Iron- monger, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Shorthand Writers' Association. An interesting innovation was introduced to this Association at their weekly meeting held at the Winmarleigh Caf4 on Wednesday night, the lady members controlling the proceedings. At the outset, hiss E. Houghton Was elected to the chair,and several of the fair sex read dictation matter on technical and other subjects, at varying rates of speed, in a very businesslike manner. The latter half of the pro- gramme was occupied by the reading by Miss Delmage of a paper written by Hiss K. Pickard, B. entitled, Ought a woman to earn her own living? " As may be imagined, such a subject was bound to create a deal of interest, and the assembly listened with great pleasure to what proved to be an extremely able paper. The writer reviewed the difficulties which in the past had beset the path of the woman who had by force of circumstances been left to depend upon herself for her livelihood, and how public opinion was gradually coming to acknowledge that a woman had a perfect right to a place in the com- mercial work of the nation, especially in such a department as shorthand and typewriting, but insisted that she should take care to thoroughly equip herself for the mental and manual daxterity required for the successful practice of these arts. An animated debate followed the reading of the paper, and the meeting terminated with a hearty vote of thanks to the ladies who had conducted what was undoubtedly a very instructive and enjoyable meeting. That the penny popular concert inaugurated last season have supplied a long felt want and are highly appreciated, there can be no doubt. The audience which which assembled in Bold-street school on Saturday evening for the first concert of the season had a thoroughly happy time and a successful series lof entertainments can safely be prophesied. The building was filled in every part and the admirable programme was t•eceived with enthusiasm. Songs were most effectively given by Miss A. Woodland, Mr. J. Willett, and Mr. D. Gittens and selections by the Apollo Quartette party delighted the audience. Miss M. Stanley played two mandoline solos with taste and skill. Features which proved exceptionally popular were the duet "When we are married" by Master W. Barlow and Miss E. Dann and the sketch Tell me pretty maiden " by members of Mr. T. Brough's , juvenile choir. Mr. Maybury was the huinourists and 'succeeded in creating great mirth. The duties of accompanist were well discharged by Mr. A. Trow. Daring an interval the Rev. J. Manning delivered a short address in which he pointed out that the concerts had passed the experimental stage and he believed they were highly appreciated. Death of Mr. R. W. Howson.

I We announce with regret the death of Mr. Richard 'Whitlock Rowson head of the firm of R. W. ROWSOII, and Son, Market Place, which took place at his resid- ence, 5, Wilson-Patten-street, on Saturday evening. Deceased (who was 52 years of age) had been in a delicate state of health for some months, but was at his office about three weeks ago. A native of Warring- ton he succeeded to the well-known business in the Market-place, originally founded by his grandfather, and subsequently carried on by his father and uncle. He had for many years been closely associated with Holy Trinity Church, having once held the office of churchwarden and at the time of his decease was a sidesman. A Conservative in politics, he had a large circle of friends both in Warrington and the district, by whom his death will be sincerely regretted. —The funeral took place at Grappenhall on Thursday when the chief mourners were Mr. Lewis R. Rowson son), Messrs. A. and G. H. Howson (brothers), Rev. E. Middleton and Mr. W. R. Lewis (brothers-in-law) Revs. A. L. Whitlock andJ. E. Beardsmorth (cousins,) Mr. James Hepherd, Rev, H. R. Wild, Rev. W. E. Glenn, Rev. T. W. Barber, Mr. R. Castle (Liverpool), Mr. W. Jones (Liverpool),and Drs. Bowdon and Lang- dale. The service was cnnductei by the Revs. E. C. E. Carleton and H. V. Particulars ol the splendid programme to be sub- mitted at the Southport Musical Festival on Wednes- day, Thursday and Friday, will be found in our advertising columns. The Rev.C.Harvey Cook will deliver an address on "The rise of democracy and its message to Liberalism" at the meeting of the Junior Liberal Association, at the Liberal Club, on Monday evening. A sale of work in connection with Wycliffe Congrega- tional Church will be held in the Memorial Buildings on Thursday. It will be opened at three o'clock by Mrs. Rylands. In the evening Mr. W. H. Payton wili give an organ recital. The Warrington Dramatic Society announce that they will produce "Dr. Wake's Patient " in January next. • Mr. E. England, one of the elective auditors for the Borough, will present a report at a meeting to be held in the C)-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Wednesday evening. Mr. James Dodds will preside at the popular concert in the Bold-street schools to-night. An excellent programme has been arranged. At his weekly meeting for men, to be held in Toft's Assembly Room on Thursday, the Rev. J. F. Matthews will deliver an address on" Religion and Sport." The annual meeting of the Stockton Heath Tree Planting Committee will be held at the 'Hall oaf 6 on Monday evening. Browning Lecture.

The third of the course of lecture on R obert Browning was delivered in the Co-operative Hall on Wednesday evening by Mr. J. A. Dale. MA. who dealt in an interesting and instructive manner with some of the poet's works. There was a fair attendance.

Meetings for Men. Owing to the pressure on our space caused by elec- tion news we have been obliged to omit the report of the Rev. J. F. Matthews' second address to men in Toft' Assembly Room on Thursday evening. There was a very good attendance and a profitable and help- ful meeting. 'Fall Through a Glass Roof. On Tuesday afternoon, James Whalley, of 25, Barnard-street, was engaged cleaning windows at Ilfessrs. Monks, Hall and Co.'s works, Liverpool-road, when he slipped and fell through a glass roof into the office, a distance of about twenty feet. It was found that his leg was broken, and he was conveyed to the Infirmary. HOUSEWIVES will have to pay more for HAMS, BACON, CHEESE AND LARD.—Advt. Sequel to a Stockton Heath Law Case. At the Warrington County Court on Thursday before his Honour Judge Shiress Will, K.C., Margaret Bates, wife of Edwin Bates, Carleton-street, Stockton Heath brought an action against Mr. W: H. J. Jenkens land Miss Turnock, executors of the will of the late Charles Higginbottorn, to recover £l4 Is. 6d. and £l7 117 s. for services rendered. Plaintiff was represented by Mr. C. H. Unsworth, defendants,being represented by Mr. A. Browne.—Plaintiff's case in regard to the first claim was that she was engaged by Mr. Higgin- bottom to look after his house and whilst she had never been paid for he: services she had had to pay a girl 3s. a week to look after her house. After the funeral she was engaged by Mr. Jenkins to look after Mrs. Fligginbottorn and the wages due for this formed the subject of the second claim.— Defendants denied that plaintiff had been engaged by Mr. Higginbottom, or by Mr. Jenkins.—Judgment was given for the plaintiff in the first cage for £l2 105. with costs and in the second case for the amount claimed with costs. Death of Mr. Samuel Dunbobbln. _

The death occurred on Thursday, under sudden circumstances, of Mr. Samuel Dunbobbin (77), of 35, Cairo-street. Deceased, who was employed by the Whitecross Company, Ltd., as a watchman was on Thursday morning, when at work, apparently in his usual health. Shortly after noon however he was seen to fall and be died before assistance could be rendered. Deceased was a prominent Co-operator and had been an active member of the Warrington Society for thirty-four years, having served on the Committee for a lengthy period. He was also widely known by reason of his active association with the local Order of Druids. In his earlier life he sought municipal honours contesting the then South-West Ward, when he was defeated by the late Alderman Hutchinson and the late Councillor Muir. In politics he was a staunch Liberal and in religion a Unitarian
