Mum THE CLocK for Good BOOTS. Advt.— A Plaintiff's Strange Admissions. A singular case was heard at the Warrington County, Conft on Thursday when an Italian, Raffo Seffino sued Bernardo Monfredi, ice cream vendor, for £l3 wages due.—Mr. Monfredi, who was repre- sented by Mr. T. S. Steel, pleaded that plaintiff had been stealing money for some time. He had had his suspicions of Seffino and hid himself under the bed in his room. He saw the plaintiff go to the cash box and take some money. The next day he and three witnesses concealed themselves and watched the plaintiff again take some money. Seffino was taxed with the theft and said he had stolen £1 17s. 6(1. Witness explained that he had missed about £lOO sad Seffino after hesitating said he might have taken £2O; perhaps he had taken £4O, and it was possible that he had taken £OO.— Plaintiff excused his admission by saying that he was afraid of being sent to gaol, as the defendant threatened, for seven years.---Afr. Monfredi said be did not want to prosecute Seffino for theft, and agreed to let him off on his signing al receipt for the wages clue to him. The receipt be produeed.—His Honour Judge Shires Wills, K.C., gave judgment for the defendant with costs.

J, R. WOOD, Piano Dealer and Tuner, 47, Old London-road., Stockton Heath.—Advt. Junior Liberal Association. A paper on "Phatham,"was given by Mr.H. Gray at the meeting of the Junior Liberal Association on Monday. The lecturer remarked that Chatham, although he came of a wealthy family,had no influenc 3 to back him up. He,passed through Eton and Oxford, but in no particular sense did he distinguish himself. At the age of 23 years he entered the arms-, but he seemed to have had no ambitio'n in that 'direction. At the age of 27 years he entered Parliament as mem- ber for Old. Sarum, one of the " pocket " boroughs. He very soon made his maiden speech, which created a profound impression upon the House, but he so roused the irony of the King by the sarcasm he used with reference to the marriage of the King's son that during the reign of George`ll. Chatham made very little headway. At that time Walpole's Administra- tion was characterized by peace and industrial develop- ment, but Chatham fought against Walpole, on account of the latter's negligence in taking steps towards the suppression of the piracy of the French and Spaniards. The result of Chatham's years of agitation in that direction was the several wars of that time including the Canadian war. In spite of the hatred of the King and the jealousy of the Court he fought his way to the front in Parliamentary life and reached the post of Prime Minister. He fought hard for purity in public life, disdaining to avail himself of the sums of money which were considered quite in keeping with the position. He was really England's first statesman who fought against bribery and corruption in public life. He devoted a considerable portion of his life towards the emancipation of India from the hands of the merchants. One of the features of his lifs was his splendid defence of the American colonies against the unjust taxation of imports. Had Chatham's 'ideas been carried out it Was probable that we should have retained those colonies.

EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.'
THE PRICE OF A DOG.

James Lancaster, of Robins Row, was summoned at Newton Petty Sessions last Thursday for keeping a dog without a licence.—P.C. Simpson found the dog at defendant's house in bed with a lad of about 14. Defendant said it was not his dog, he had sold it for the price of 2 pints of beer, at the f' Bottom House," to Thomas Donovan. It went back to his house, but was not bis.—Donovan deposed to buying it and said he had lost a former dog by poison, and kept this one with the licence he had for the former one.—The ques- tion arose whether he was entitled to do that. Ultim- ately the summons against Lancaster was withdrawn.

div.head: BAKER'S FINED.
div.p: BAKER'S FINED.

John Hatton, grocer and baker, of Fairclougn-street, Earlestown, was summoned at Newton Petty Sessions last Thursday for selling bread otherwise than by weight —Mr. Wilson, for the County Council, said Inspector Shepherd sent a man named Hiltox into Mr. Hatton's shop, where a loaf was sold to him for 21,d. without being weighed. Mr. Shepherd then went into the shop and had a conversation with the defend Int's wife, who i practically admitted that the loaf • was not weighed. The loaf was three-quarters of an ounce shor of 2lbs. weight.—The Chairman said the defendant ha been a tradesman in Earlestown a great many years, and was highly respected.—Mr. Hatton : Thirty-six years, sir.— The Chairman : But you have been up twice before for the same offence, and I am convinced it is only negligence.—Mr. Hatton : It is only negligence, sir.— Fined ss. and costs.—Emily Ann Heap was summoned for a similar offence at her shop in Wargrave-road, and pleaded that she did not know that she had to weigh the loaf. She had only been in business since last December.—The Bench required the defendant to pay the costs, and advised her to remember what she had to do in future.

div.head: ST HELENS._
div.p: ST HELENS._
BEEN IN TWENTY-THREE ASYLUMS.

James Horner, who was charged at St. Helens on Monday with begging, made a very singular defence. Horner said he was a compositor, and belonged to Derby, but he was not responsible for his actions. Police-constable Whittaker said that Horner said he had been in twenty-three asylums. The Chief Constable : He must have been in all the asylums then. Horner was remanded for medical examination.
ST. HELENS LIBRARIES.I w

The monthly meeting of the St. Heleus Libraries Committee was held on Wednesday. The librarian re- ported an increase of 2,6'83 in the issues of books.— Councillor Foote, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. ' Lacey as chairman, referred to his lifelong work on behalf of the libraries of the town. Their chairman took a very deep interest in library work,and he thought that the interest he took and the work he did in that way caused him to enjoy such good health at an advanced age.—The Chairman, in rely, said he agreed with Hr. Footethat the taking part in public life did assist materially in prolonging life, for if he sat at home and did nothing he was sure he would not be as well as he was. They were engaged in a noble work and he rejoiced at the great progress they had made and the fact that people were increasingly reading a better class of liteiature year by year.

div.head: ALLEGED THEFT OF SACKS.
div.p: ALLEGED THEFT OF SACKS.

!Ellen Watson, a Liverpool general dealer, was charged at St. Helens, on Monday, along with Joseph Wedgwood, aged fourteen, and a man named Patrick , Marooney, with stealing a bundle of thirty-three empty , flour sacks, value Is. 6d. each.—Superintendent Baxen- dale said that on the 9th inst.a carter drew up his lorry and horses in front of the Angel Inn, at Eccleston-lane Ends, and went inside. Shortly afterwards Mrs. Watson drove up with her cart. It was alleged that they snatched two bundles oil the lurry and threw them on the cart and drove away. The carter ran out and managed to secure one of the bundles. The police later found that the bags had been sold for -Id. each at a Liverpool marinestore on the 12th inst. When charged, they denied the theft, and said the carter sold them the sacks.—The three defendants were remanded fora week

div.head: RUFFIANISAI IN ST. HELENS STREETS.
div.p: RUFFIANISAI IN ST. HELENS STREETS.

Joseph 111`Naughton,of G7,osford-street,was remanded at St. Helens on Monday on a charge of unlawfully wounding Mrs. Sarah Woodward, of 29, Grange Park- road.—The Chief Constable said the man was a rough character, and he had been guilty of a most cowardly and unprovoked assault. About 9.30 on Saturday night a man named Charles Wood was standing outside the Robin Hood public-house in Tontine-street, when M`Naugiiton went across the road to him and asked him to have a drink. Wood declined, and prisoner went away, but a few minutes later he came running swiftly along the street and struck Wood violently in the jaw. He con- tinued his career, an struck Mrs. Woodward with all his might full in the nose, knocking her down like a ninepin. He ran on, and Mr. Woodward, who had been I quietly walking along the street. tried to catch M`Naughton, but failed. Mrs. Woodward was in a 1 delicate state of health. Dr. Masson attended her, and I said she would be in bed for some time. She was ' suffering from cuts on the face and head, and from con- cussion of the brain, and the shock of the blow and the fall likely to produce very serious results.—Evidence was given, upon which the magistrates ordered a week's remand.

div.head: CUERDEN HALL SALE.
div.p: THE CUERDEN HALL SALE.

Theseventeen days sale at Cuerden Hall, Thelwall, the late residence of Mr. :R. A. Naylor, was commenced on Monday afternoon by Messrs. Capes, Dunn, and Pitcher, the well-known Manchester auctioneers. Con- siderable interestwas aroused locally and in the dealers, circle, and buyers were present from all parts of the country. The catalogue is a bulky volume of 223 pages and gives particulars of nearly 4,000 lots, consisting of a very large selection of old English pottery and porcelain, specimens of continental and oriental china, furniture in pld oak, mahogany, Bombay-wood, &c, including many examples of real Chippendale. The sale commenced at one o'clock each day during the week, and for the first two days some good prices were realised, particularly for the china, considering that most of it was not of great value to connoisseurs and collectors.

Some of the most interesting and valuable lots sold were as follows :—First day : Old Dresden china candelabra, with floral encrustations and branches for six lights, £l7. Pair Indian cleverly carved, wood fixtures, 56m. high, and supporting an 18in. deep-tone gong, £4 ss. Spanish mahogany cabinet, 6ft. high by 4ft. 9in., £7. Display cabinets in dark mahogany, sft. high by 4ft. Gin, wide, £l5 each. Old oak chest, inscribed "Peter Breck, 801t0n,1764," £5 10s. Dresden China table, £4. Soldier in armour, £2 ss. Pair old richly chased Ormulu candelebra for nine lights each, £5 2s. 6d. Pair curious lead figures of Cupid, £9 ss. Stuffed lioness, £2 10s. Infant bacchanal with pitcher, £7 15s. Bronze figure, La Petite Savoyarde, £9. Crown Derby dessert service, £6 15s. Second day's sale : Pair of Oriental vases, 54in. high, £3 10s. Pair of jardinieres, lain. high. enamelled in colours with birds, foliage, and flowers, the insides decorated with fish, £5O. Dresden china centrepiece, 39in. high, £9 10s. Fine old Worcester blue and white tea and coffee service £lB 158. Sevres china vases and covers, £l7. Royal blue, green and richly gilt Spode china tea and coffee service, £7 15s. Spode tea and coffee service, £4 2s. Gd. China mug, 545. Chelsea jug, £3 17s. Gd. The oil paintings and engravings came under the hammer on Wednesday, but there was great disappoin- ment at the prices realised. Many of the pictures are alleged to be inferior copies of old masters, and where hundreds of pounds were expected to be bid, shillings only were offered. The sale will be continued ou Monday at one o'clock, and the following days, Saturday excepted. Monday's sale will consist of the furniture, coins, etc. in the Oak Room.

OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. Services for Sunday. Bold-street Wesleyan Church: Preachers, 10.30, Rev S. Pitt ; 6.30, Rev. J. Manning. Bewsey-road Wealeyan Church : Preachers, 10.30, Rev. J. Manning ; 6.30, Rev. S. Pitt. Golborne-street Baptist Church: Preacher, 10.30 and 6.30, Rev. E. E. Lovell, president of the Shropshire Association of Baptist Churches. Latchford Baptist Church : Preacher, 10.30 and 6, Rev. J. F. Matthews. Subjects : Morning," Waiting for power " ; evening, "An old, old story." Wycliffe Congregational Church : Harvest thanks- giving. Preacher, Rev. G. W. Gervis, Golborne. Morning anthem, "0 Lord, how manifold" ; evening " The Heavens are telling." Wycliffe P.S.A. : Meeting 3.0. The chair will be taken by Captain Crosfield, and an address will be delivered bp Councillor Evans. Soloist: Mr.. War- burton.

Young Free Churchmen's Auxiliary. Mr. C. E. Parker was announced to deliver an address at the meeting of the Free Churchmen's Auxiliary held in Bold-street Church Parlour last even- ing, but he had earlier in the day to journey to Scotland. In his abseace the paper which he had prepared, was read by the Rev. J. F. Matthews. It dealt in a hithly interesting way with the career of William Lloyd Garrison, the pioneer of the abolition of slarery in America.

div.head: AN AUTUMN WARNING.
div.p: AN AUTUMN WARNING.
Bile Beans the Best Defence Against
Liver Chills.
Latchford Baptist Church.

The anniversary services in connection with the above church were held on Sunday, the preacher being the ' Rev. Stuart Caldwell, of Oldham, who preached in the morning to a large congregation. The choir in a very able manner rendered the anthem "The Lord is my Shepherd" ( afacfarren). In the afternoon a musical service was held, Mr. George Wells occupying the chair. The choir were again heard to advantage in their rendering of the cantata " Sowing and reaping." In the evening the Rev. Stuart Caldwell preached from the text" Speak, Lord, for Thy servant heareth." The anthem was Praise the Lord" (Clare). Mr. Peter Harrison presided at the organ. The collections were in aid of the church funds.

div.head: St. Paul's Church.
div.p: St. Paul's Church.

_ - - There were large congregations at the above church I on Sunday, when the harvest thanksgiving services were continued. The preacher in the morning was the Rev. H. A. Lester, vice-princip il of the Training College, who said they should think of their privileges as a Christian people in a Christian land. When they thought of the devotion and self-sacrifice of their fathers in handing ‘own to them the pure and undefiled Scriptures —the faith once delivered to the saints—would they allow these privileges to be taken from them and the Bible banished from their national schools ? If their 1 hearts were thankful would they not show it by a deter- mination that nothing, so far as they could help it, should take from their children their undoubted birth- right to be taught and brought up in the nurture and fear of the Lord ? A children's service was held at. 2.15, and a united Bible class service at three o'clock, the preacher being the Rev. B. Percival. The Vicar preached in the evening to a very large congregation. The collections, were in aid of the restoration fund.

div.head: _Christian Endeavour Anniversary.
div.p: _Christian Endeavour Anniversary.

The Anniversary of the Christian Endeavour Society in connection with the Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church was celebrated on Sunday. The preacher fpr the day was the minister, the Rev. C. L. Stowe. Preach- ing in the morning from the text, " What do ye more than others ?" Mr. Stowe, said Christian parents, should not only educate, clothe, and feed their children but they should instil into them the great principles of religion, and be especially interested in their spiritual progress. At the afternoon Sunday school, Miss Taylor (who had attended the World's Christian Endeavour Conference at Geneva), gave an address on " The development of the spiritual faculties." Various prizes were presented to the scholars, after which the Super- intendent (Mr. Bistle), on behalf of the teachers and scholars, presented to one of the Endeavourers (Mr. Cooper) a pair of vases and flower pot on the occasion of his recent marriage. Mr. Cooper suitably responded. —There was a large gathering at the evening service, when the Rev. C. L. Stowe based his discourse on the text "No root in themselves." The collections for the day amounted to £2 6s. 7id. A tea was held on Monday evening, followed by a devotional service. The Pastor occupied the chair, and the speakers were Miss B. Lees and the Rev. J. S. Hughes. Miss Lees spoke on "Salvation and Service," while Mr. Hughes's address was on " Ideals." Miss A. Woodland rendered effec- tively the solo " I know that my Redeemer liveth."

Stockton Heath Wesleyan Anniversary. The anniversary services in connection with the Stockton Heath Wesleyan Methodist Church, were held on Sunday and were highly successful. Sermons were preached morning and evening, by the Rev. R. Wilkins Rees, of Fleetwood, and formerly of the Warrington circuit and special anthems were rendered by the choir in an admirable manner. In the afternoon a musical service was held presided over by Mr. F. A. Harris. Selections were given with effect by Miss Alice Wood- land (soprano), Miss Lily Fairhurst (conttalto), Mr. S. Hassall (tenor), and Mr. G. Gough (bass). The collec- tions were in aid of the new trust fonds. -

On Monday evening th-e-ann'QucenWe'gational gather- ing was held. The proceedings opened with a tea in the schoolroom, to which a fairly large number of friends sat down. After tea, the party adjourned to the church, where public meeting was bold ? presided over by Mr. James Dodds.

_ The Chairman, in opening the proceedings appealed to those present not only to support Nonconformity, but temperance work. Tt was much needed in Warring- ton and he hoped therefore that the next work he under- cook would be connected with it and that they would not be behind in holding temperance meetings in Warrington. The Rev. ft. Wilkins Rees, who had a hearty recep- tion, said he was sorry that there was still a debt upon the building, but he hoped that they would soon sweep it off. They had had great assistance from Mr. Dodds —(applanse)--but he would remind them that money was not everything. A church that had plenty of money and no religion was no church at all. They should all remember that not only were attendance and , prayer needed, but they should pray hard and work hard pray as if they could do nothing by themselves, and work as if they could do everything. He was not thorn to glorify Methodism, but there were striking excell- encies. Having put their hands to the Methodist plough, they ought never to look back. (Applause.) Having, made the Methodist Church their choice, they should, seek to do all that, they could to further its interests. (Applause.) Mr. .T. Upson, junior circuit steward, said they had now magnificent premises at Stockton Heath and many facilities and advantages, and he hoped they would give, prominence to the spiritual side of their work. If they did that they would never have any difficulty in money matters. (Applause.) The Rev. Sidney Pitt also addressed the meeting. A collection was taken in aid of the trust funds.

SEIGEL'S SYRUP.

When you feel "a bit ran down" don't neglect the warning. Don't think it is nothing, that it will pass off, or that you will "shake it off." If you have an exceptionally strong constitution you may perhaps shake it oil for a time ; but—it will return, and ere long you will find yourself in the grip of acute indiges- tion. This eras the experience of Mrs. Mary Ann Frobisher, 22, Armitage Street; Castleford, Yorks, but Mother Seigel's Syrup restored her to health. Writing on May 21st, 1906, she says : " Some ten years ago I was kept so busy, having both a business and a house to look after, that meal-times never came round for me. Something in my hand, eaten while at work. was all I could manage generally. Of coursip this told on me. I felt a bit run down and tired. My tongue was coated in the morning. ond there was a bad taste in my mouth. "Then 'got worse. My head ached, oh, such a lot, and so often,and there were sharp stabbing pains in my side —it was awful! Little balls of light used to dance before my eyes. A doctor prescribed for me, but I got no better. "At last, on a neighbour's advice I got some Mother Seigel's Syrup and then relief came. I improved rapidly and soon was completely cured."

div.p: LOCAL CHURCHES.
Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.l

The usual meeting was held on Sunday, wheVlr Cotton presided awl said he occupied the chair as an encouragement to others to do likewise, and so help the Secretary in carrying out his arrangements for these happy meetings. Mr. J. Harrison of Liverpool spoke upon" Liberty." He referred to the liberty won for us by Oliver Cromwell and others, who fought for religious liberty. Let us. he said, have liberty from priestcraft whilst allowing liberty to others who did not agree with our faith and doctrine. He detested men who would get np a demonstration against the faith of others. Men who thought more of their millions and the sword than the faith in the lowly Christ. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind and so serve Christ Who went about doing good. He urged all present, especially young men, to tight against intem- perance, and all passions which destroyed the highest in man, thereby robbing him of his liberty, because these things made him a bondsman. Mr. William Hayes and :11r. D. Owen also took part in the meeting. Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bet., presided at the organ. The Secretary welcomed four new members, the total now being 491. The organ fund contribution was 19s. 4d. The Secretary has received from a friend of the P.S.A. ,One guinea towards the organ fund this week.

Mr. Fieldhouse is heard to less advantage I in the pretty hailed" In babyhood upon her lap I lay," 7 , the honours of which are divided with Mr. Bibby as I Lord Monntararat. As the Earl of Mountararat Mr. IJ. W. Bibby is to be congratulated upon another signal succeSs. His dignified and commanding stage presence ! eminently fits him for the part of the blue blooded ! aristocrat whose very pronounced opinions as to the , sacredness of the British aristocracy are so much to the . fore. Mr. Bibb j possesses the virture of a clear enuncia- tion. Every word he utters can be distinctly heard. He throws himself into several concerted and solo 1 vocal items with great zest, interpreting that flue and spirited song "When Britain really ruled the waves" / with such gusto as to quite take the audience by storm I No wonder that throughout the week the song has been one of the great hits of the opera and has gained vociferous encores. Mr. J. Rabbitt is . a great favourite with the patrons of the ' Warrington operas and as Earl Tolloller, the rival lover with the Earl of Mountararat, he worthily upholds the high opinion we have formed of him in previous enterprises. Possessed of a pure-toned and powerful tenor voice he delights the audience with a

fine rendering of "Spurn not the lowly born " which has proved exceedingly popular during the week. Mr. Rabbitt ably brings out the subtle humour of the part and his acting throughout is marked by a confidence betokening careful study. A particularly amusing passage, occasioning a great deal of mirth, is that in which the two noble earls disingenuously argue as to who should waive his claim to the hand of Phyllis in favour of his companion suitor. In the "Barcarolle" iii which the two learls in turn sue for Phyllis's favour —the opening solo by Tolloller beginning "Of all the young ladies I knoae this pretty young lady's the fairest "—Mr. Rabbitt finds further opportunity of dis- tinguishing himself. The centre of humour in the opera is of course the Lord Chancellor and this role affords Mr. C. P. Gough a splendid opportunity of dis- playing his natural aptitude for interpreting Gilbertian comedy. Nothiro, but praise can be bestowed on his presentment of this important character, a performance whioh has won the warmest encomiums each evening. Mr. Gough can be the embodiment of either official dignity and austerity or of refreshing playfulness and agility just as occasion demands, and be brings Lome to the audience in the most laughable way the ludicrousness of the position of a very suscaptible Chancellor who has to sit in his Court all day "giving agreeable girls away," the while himself hopelessly smitten by the charms of one of his attractive wards. The song which follows immediately upon his pompous entry—" The law is the true embodi- ment of everything that's excellent "—goes with a delightful swing, and the same remark applies to "When I went to the Bar as a very young man," hi which his mimicry of professional men is exceedingly fanny. Mr. Gough's most successful effort, how- ever, is that amazing patter song "When you're lying awake with a dismal headache," descriptive lof the horrors of nightmare. This song, with its weird and wonderful dream story, has proved especially popular, although all three/ songs I have been encored nightly. The sudden transition I from the farcical to the intensely dramatic involved in the incidents which bring the opera to a close is exceptionally well realized by Mr. Gough and Miss Henshall, and the varying emotions with which the Chancellor listens to lolanthe's pathetic appeal and the subsequent. startling disclosure of her relationship to him have been so vividly depicted as to very deeply impress the audience. One of the most captivating features of the opera is the merry trio with the refrain " Faint heart never won fair lady" in which the Chan- cellor, Lord Monntamrat and Lord Tolloller share the honours. The melody is one of the brightest and most vivacious in the opera, and when the three distinguished participants throw austerity to the winds and indulge in a sprightly dance the hilarity of the . situation becomes contagious. Delighted applause has greeted this item, and so unmis- takable has been the demand for" more" that the trio has been repeated several times at each perform- ance. As the dainty principal fairies Celia, Leila and Fleta, Miss Marie Houghton, Mrs. C. Garton Stone and Miss Alice Daunt have comparatively little to do, but they acquit themselves in these singing parts as well as in the business of picturesquely posing in the near ground, most satisfactorily. The duet In vain to us you plead" by Leila and Celia, has proved one of the few disappointments of the opera. How this choice number fails to impreis the audience as it should do it is not easy to discover,and we are are inclined to think some uncertainties in the orchestra are largely account- able for the want of precision and" go " which should characterise its rendering. Miss Garnett Ball is to be congratulated upon a very promising debut as the Queen of the Fairies. She comports herself with befitting dignity and is occasionally quite dramatic in uphold- ing the authority of her Queendom and her subjectk in opposition to the autocratic peers. In a rich con- tralto voice of ,good compass. she sings " Oh, foolish fay "which, with Its pretty Chorus, listened to witn wrapt attention,is regularly followed byan encore each evening. Mr. Walter A. Clay also makes a first appear- ance as Private Willis into which part he infuses an unaffected drollery which mightilyamuses the audience, scoring a notable success each evening with the fine song When all night long " with its quaint soliloquy upon the political propensities of each new and rising generation. Sung with great verve this number—one conceived in Gilbert's happiest vein—has si ightly found favour and has as often been I ntlausi- astically encored. The most delightful of the concerted items is undoubtedly the quartette "In friendship's name " in which Lord Mountararat, Lord Tolloller, Phyllis and Private Willis are associa- ated. In this veritable gem of harmony the voices have been balanced to a nicety, the blending of the whole in masses of unaccompanied vocal harmony so charming the audience each evening as to make repetitions of this number unavoidable.

Of the chorus Work it is possible to speak in terms of unreserved praise. Not only have the various masses of voices been well adjusted in relation to each other but the singing of one and all has been marked by a pre- cision and a careful attention to marks of expression which is highly praiseworthy. Nor have we any hut words of admiration for the appearance ea masse of the ladies' chorus. The appearance in the Arcadian glade of the fairy gathering is a charming spectacle—a bevy of female loveliness, in costumes of the most delicate and sheeny fabrics, delighting the eye both in form and colour from the moment of the initial unfolding of the opera. A most picturesque pageant in the first act is the March of the Peers which, to the _strains of triumphal music, is chars° terized by great pomp and splendour. Spectacularly and musically, however, the scene which most vividly impresses itself on the audience is that in which 'the first act reaches its climax. Here the fairies with uplifted wands threaten the peers who kneel as If begging for mercy, and the curtain is rung down as Phyllis, spurned by her distressed lover, falls fainting into the air of Lord l'tionntararat and Lord Tolloller. The audie e has at this point been nightly moved to a storm of ap ause and on many evenings the closing chorus has had to, be repeated in response to insistent demands. A most touching passage is that in which lolanthe dis- closes her identity as his wife to the Lord Chancellor, the fairies in the distance breaking into a wierd, wailing chorcs,and later entering to seal the doom of one who has for a second time broken her vows to the Fairy Queen. The credit for the unqualified success of " lolanthe " as for similar achievements in past years must be divided in pretty equal proportions between the opera committee's capable and hard-working musical director and conductor, Mr. Frank H. Crossley, and the similarly accomplished and indefatigable dramatic instructor and stage manager, Mr. Thornley Dodge. Those outside the management of such enterprises can form little idea of the strenuous work involved In carrying to a succes- fnl conclusion a work of this kind. As mentioned in our interview with Mr. Crossley last week, that gentle- man is justly proud not only of his principals and chorus but of his orchestra which latter holds the almost unique position in ventures of this kind of being entirely amateur. Of the service rendered by this fine body of instrumentalists under Mr. R. H. Pearson's leader- ship, we can speak generally in terms of high commendation. It is unavoidable under the cir- cumstances that there should at times be moments of obscurity and indefiniteness in the playing of an orchestra so constituted, and, though the strings were not by any means beyond reproach, it was noticeable that the chief defects arose, as might be expeoted,from the difficulty of bringing the wind instruments into complete agreement amongst themselves and in unison with the stringed instruments forming the staple material of the orchestra. Much, however, of the orchestral work was nevertheless admirable both when the whole forces were simultaneously engaged, as in the Peers' March,the overture and the finale to the first act, and when subtler effects were to be sought as in the love-duets between Phyllis and Strephon, the Fairy Queen's song and lolanthe's most touching ballad near the close of the work.

The stage-manager had obviously spent immense trouble—involving also, no doubt, the exercise of some exemplary patience—in marshalling the choral members in the numerous striking and compli- cated stage movements and the dances for which " lolanthe " offers splendid opportunity and scope. Especially effective from this point of view were the groupings and evolutions of the company in the first act, the close of which caught on with the audience to such an extent that no denial would be taken of a repetition of its climacteric conclusion. All which, coupled with the quite professional, and apparently perfectly natural, movements and deportment of the principal actors and actresses themselves,—for which of course the stage manager is responsible—redounds greatly to Mr. Thornley-Dodge's credit. It was there- fore no empty compliment when along with calls before the curtain each evening for all the principals there was a loud demand for the appearance of both Mr. Dodge and Mr. Crossley. It is due to say that the whole of the greatly admired dresses for the ladies chorus as well as sotne for the principals were made bye dress-maker in the ranks of the chorus itself, Miss Id ipkiss of Bewsey- road. Other equally beautiful costumes for the ladies were the elections or Messrs. W. Hodgkinspn Ltd., and Miss Hall of Bold-street, Warrington. The gentlemen's dresses were from the opera committee's regular costumiers, Messrs. Burkinshaws of Liverpool. For the elaborate and effective make-up of the whole com- pany and for the various wigs &c.. Messrs. Birch Browne and Son are responsible, while the much admired scenery and the beautiful limelight illumina- tion were supplied and managed by Messrs. P. Is Maistre und Co., of Manchester. A meed of praise for carrying through the whole project should not be withheld from the opera committee which comprises Mr. H. Bond, Mr. J. W. Bibby, Mr. F. H. Crossley, Mr. W. H. Payton Mus. Bac. and Mr. J. Newcombe, the last the hard-worked yet ever kindly hon. secretary and treasurer. Mr. Payton has acted as a most capable pianist throughout the very numerous rehearsals leading up to the week's magnificent success.

div.head: " lOLANTHE."
div.p: " lOLANTHE."
SUCCESSFUL PERFORMANCES BY MEMBERS OF THE MUSICAL ~. SUETY.

Can Gilbert and Sullivan be successfully revived? Warrington, we think, has given a conclusive answer to this question which some would have us believe is fraught with doubts and difficulties as far as London, the horns of the famous operas, is concerned. Here for the past four years we have had Gilbert and Sullivan's works roduced with a success which proves that the pro ncial taste, at any rate, has not entirely degenerate as seems to be the case with the metropolis, but that it can still appreciate and enjoy the old favourites when they are adequately presented. It is therefore more than surprising to us that, in 1 London the revival of the operas associated with the Savoy. is looked upon as a somewhat hazardous venture. Warrington, in common with many other provincial towns, has shown unmistakably that light opera of the right sort can be made to pay and that, moreover, it is acceptable in the highest degree to the public. Thanks to the enterprise of certain of the bolder spirits in the Warrington Musical Society,who launched the project at a critical period as a means of placing the society upon a better financial footing and at the same time of providing bright and pleasant entertainment, Warringtonians have been afforded the opportunity of seeing four of the most popalar of the Gilbert and Sullivan collaborations staged on a complete and entirely adequate scale. The measure of support accorded has exceeded the most sanguine expectations and the musical society's opera is now welcomed as one of the happiest events of the local musical season. That it may long continue as an annual institution is, we are sure, the sincere wish of a large number of the townspeople. "lolanthe" has been presented at the Parr Hall every evening this week, and the opera contingent of the society is to b., congratulated upon the achieve- ment of another notable triumph. When the curtain was rung down at the close of the first performance, on Monday evening it was to the accompaniment of the enthusiastic acclaims of an audience which fille4every part of the ground floor of the building. Prificipals came forward to receive well-deserved ovations and the general verdict may be summed up in the over- heard eulogy: "A delightful opera, well played." Throughout the week there have liteen crowded attend- ances, the pleasure given being manifested in no half-hearted degree, and we believe we are right in saying that none but the most pleasant remembrances will be retained of " lolanthe." It was a commendable. idea which prompted the committee to devote Monday's and Friday's net proceeds to the infirmary extension fund. Such an eminently deserving undertaking could not fail to appeal to the community, and the response to this invitation to further a good cause has been very gratifying. Among the series ,of operas which the genius of Gilbert and Sullivan gave to the world, "lolanthe " holds quite a distinctive place. The Gilbertian imagination has had full play in ,his fairy romance,and the complications which arise in it are as novel and original, as they are highly amusing. While there is an absence of the boisterous comic element, subtle and refined humour is by no means lacking, and the dramatic vein is strongly en evidfice. The li' dded --Qin which, often s' ;liar
The Examiner, Saturday, October 20, 1906.

div.head: Warrington P.S.A.
div.p: Warrington P.S.A.

There was an excellent attendance at an open meeting of the Warrington Society which was held on Sunday. Councillor Clegg presided, and Mr. G. Davey-Smith was the speaker. Mr. Ernest Walker rendered two solos, " Abide with me " and " Thou'rt passing hence," in a very cre.ditable manner. Mr. Pownall was the accompanist. Ile president (11. r. G. W. Jones) also took part in the meeting.

div.head: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
div.p: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
LADY ABERDARE.

Lady Aberdare the prospective mother-in- laiv of Miss Camille Clifford !—has a positive horror of the present-day democracy, and espe- cially of that—form of it which introduces walk- ing ladies. and ladies from the chorus, into the Peerage, says the Bystander. She has several children, the youngest of whom is still in the nursery, while her eldest daughter married, two years ago, Lord Newport, and ill one day, in the ordinary course of events, become Countess of Bradford Devoted to the quiet life of the country and to her children, Lady Aberdare's ideas on marriage,, like those of most domes- ticated wo,nen, are conservativ.s and not exactly broad. Her views, therefore, on her son's en- gagement may better be imagined than de- scribed. An aristocrat herself, Lady Aberdare has never yet found either the time or the in- clination to assimilate the modern ideas which make all men and women equal, and so her son's choice of a wife is, to say the least of it, incom- prehensible to her. FASHIONABLE FUR Co.

Pictured in our illustration is a charmingly- pretty little fur coat of the latest and most modish type. It might be most successfully achieved in sealskin, musquash seal, electric seal, or caracal, the choice, of course, being inogulated by

the tasty and means of the wearer. The coat it- self is of the Russian type, belted at the waist, the fur pouching a little over the belt, and finished with little hip. basques. The front is opened to display , a jaunty little waistcoat of some delicately-hued velvet or cloth, elaborately trimmed with narrow silk braid. The edges of the coat are bordered with a narrow band of ermine. The sleeves, of full length, are moderate in size, and are finished with turn-back cuffs of the fur.

div.head: DRESS AT THR OPERA.
div.p: DRESS AT THR OPERA.

The Opera is again a rendezvous for smart people, says a fashion writer in the Globe. Sit- ting in the stalls, one sees some wondrous heads; nor do we women have it all our own way; there are upstanding brushes above manly counten- ances or hyacinthine, but shiny, curls framing the faces of others which are in contrast to the well-groomed and brilliantined heads of gilded youth of our own little islands, and shew the owners to be foreigners. However, it is with the women that our eyes are ever most engaged. A dark lady in a bOx with the Spanish Ambas- sador the other evening had her hair dressed high and right over her forehead, tapering down to a point almost reaching her nose. From the puff on the top two glittering vyjngs reared up, and very effective they proved. " In the stalls before us vv as a head of hair quite fair and like spun silk in text&e., It was puffed out at the back, and dressed almost flatly at the top. Clear tortoiseshell or French horn combs were used, with heads carved and jewelled. No high hair ornament was worn. A handsome blonde in the same row with us had her shining locks slightly waved, divided in the centre, and drawn down at either side, while glittering spangled white wings rose at either side. A lovely young mar- ried lady behind us. wore ' nothing in her pretty brown hair, which was dressed low. She wore a lovely long coat of dark blue satin most be embroidered in a raised design, and her dress was black. There is practically no fashion in hair-dressing; it is a case of individual choice. The combs worn now are exceedingly pretty, however, and almost everyone can choose those of a kind to match or agreeably contrast with the odour of -their hair.

div.head: VELVETEEN DRESS.
div.p: VELVETEEN DRESS.

Velvet and velveteen are again to be very much worn during the coming winter, and a dress of brown velveteen is illustrated here. It is one that could be adapted for semi-evening wear as well as an afternoon gown by having different blouses to wear beneath the velveteen bodice. The one shown in our illustration is of cream imitation Irish lace, mounted over a foundation of cream chiffon. The dress has a circular-shaped yoke, trimmed with golden-

For after- noon wear the blouse could be of golden-brokvn silk, finished with long tight-fitting cuffs.

div.head: LONDON'S OLDEST WOIUN.
div.p: LONDON'S OLDEST WOIUN.

There is at present living in the St • Pancras Union Infirmary Mrs. Sarah Lamb, who has just celebrated her 104th birthday, and is believed to be the oldest subject of the King in London. Al- though very infirm, Mrs Lamb is still in the full possession of all her faculties. She was born at Ramsgate, and when a little girl was brought to London, where she has resided ever since.

Shakespeare's Place in Literature.

The members of the Literary and Philosophical Society held their first meeting of the session on Monday evening, when Mr. J. T. Foard, barrister, of Liverpool, who is well known in Warrington as the revising barrister, read a paper on " The proper place of Shakespeare in Literature." Alderman Bennett (president) presided over a small attendance. Mr. Foard said the verdict of the ordinary Englishman upon the merits of her distinguished countryman was easily expressed. It was that Shakespeare was the greatest poet that they knew of and was head and shoulders above all other competitors. Shakespeare was essentially, in reference to universal literature,the Christian poet of all the ages. Shakespeare had no discoverable personality ; he offered no views of his own, he had no doctrinal opinions, was only the exponent of nature and moi ality, but still/ his plays were the highest spirit of Christianity ; its ethics, its tolerance, forbearance, charity, homage for feminine chastity were, in a sentence, convoyed in the very spirit of and illustrated in their teaching the Sermon on the-Mount. This was his (Mr. Foard's) chief and final claim for their national poet— as the foremost man of all ages, and the enlightening spirit of the universe.' He was the most perfect and accomplished of all writers. (Applause). A hearty vote of thanks las accorded the essayist on the proposition of Mr. Charles White, seconded by 7 Mr. E. J. Hall, and sup- ported by Mr. A. J. Jolley, Mr. Lofthouse, Mr. Woodcock, Mr. Madeley, and the President.

div.head: MY DEAR CHILDREN,
div.p: MY DEAR CHILDREN,

I am very sorry that I cannot announce the result of the boys' competition, as I have been so busy. I will do so next week for cer- tain, and the girls' the following week, blit I must tell you all that I am very satiefled, and think you have all done remarkably well. lam sure those that have gained the prizes wilt be delighted as they are extra nice ones this time.

I -am now making arrangements for a new competition for the girls. This will be mak- ing articles of clothing for the poor. I will give definite instructions next week, so be sure and get the paper. You will all remember that last year we had a similar competition, and it was most successful; many poor children were very delighted with what you so kindly made for them: so I feel quite certain that every one of you will send something that will help to •make some little child happy and warm. This week prizes have been sent to George Kirk and Gladys Knight for their contributions, which you will see printed below. I hope they will be pleased with the nice boxes of Fry's chocolates I have sent.
I think I will close my letter for this week so with all good wishes from
UNCLE N.
Dear Uncle Ned,—l am sending you a piece o: poetry called
WHEN DADDY WAS A BOY. I'm very, very naughty, And I play most awful tricks. My Daddy says he wasn't half

As bad when he was six. He never ran away from school, Nor broke his pretty toy— They simply couldn't do such things When daddy was a boy. They never put a scuttleful Of coals on Kitty's tail, Nor tackled dogs to empty cans To hear them yelp and wail; Nor stood the cat in walnut shells
To see her jump for joy, Nor cripple. frogs, or anything

. , When Daddy was a boy. Then what's the use of pussy cats, Or coals, or cans, or dogs, Or kittens, or of walnut shells, Or croaking, thrilling frogs? And why should not my Sunday clothes Be freshened up with paint? But Daddy never did such things,
For Daddy was a saint. But if they never lost themselves, Nor greased their hair with glue, Nor speckled sister's frock with ink,

Nor chopped themselves in two, Nor stirred the beehive with their sticks, Nor howled for very joy. I s'pose I'm very wicked. Not fit on earth to stay— In fact, if I must be so good, I'd rather fly away. If all that Daddy tells me Is the truth without alloy, I guess they didn't have much fun When Daddy was a boy. With all good wishes for the "Corner's" cess, I femain, your loving nephew, GEORGE KIRK.
Buc,

Dear Uncle Ned,—l was very surprised and pleased to receive the book, The Basket of Flowers," from you this morning. I have never read it, but Mother has, and she enjoyed it immensely, as I expect I shall, for I love reading. I hope you will like the story, which I have made uP myself, called "Lost and Found," and will think it suitable or the "Corner." Do you not think that, if you decide to print it, it had better be put in a little bit each week until it Is finished, as I am afraid it is very long. You will be pleased to hear that I have satisfactorily passed in - the Oxford Exam. (Preliminary Grade).
Yours truly, LUCY FITZPATRICK.
[Many thanks, Lucy, for your story. I am going to read it, and hope to make a serial of it.

div.head: LOST DOLL.
div.p: THE LOST DOLL.

Has anyone seen a big doll? I've hunted and hunted all day, First over the garden, and then through the house, Do you think that she could run away? I'd never believe she could go very far, Her feet are so slender and small That she hardly can stand, while her legs are so weak

That she 'most always leans 'gainst the wall. She's the prettiest dolly, with red, rosy cheeks, And eyes of a beautiful brown; And when I lost her was dressed in her best, Her very best pink satin gown.
GRANDMOTHER S BIRTHDAY.
"To-morrow will be grandmother's birthda. said Mary to her sister Lena as they were pl

ay- - e shall have nothing to - give her," said Lena, dolefully. "The spring is so long in corning that there is not even a snow- drop out yet. Our rich cousins, however, will be sure to get some lovely flowers." "Dear grandmother • knows that we, too, would give them if we could," answered Mary in her soft voice. But Lena only tossed her head and replied, "I don't like to be outdone."

, That afternoon their Aunt Jenny, who lived with their grandmother, Came down to see the two little girls. When her visit was over, she gave each of her nieces a bright little golden coin that they might buy nosegays for the mor- row, and also have something to spend on them- selves.

In this way their difficulty was overcome. So they made up their minds to visit Simon, the florist, who grew flowers all the year round in his glass houses, and get from him some of his prettiest flowers.

In the morning, as soon as breakfast was over, Lena and Mary turned their steps in the direction of Simon's garden, falking gaily of the flowers they meant to choose. Lena thought of buying a nosegay that would out- shine those of her cousins. Mary's wish was to show her grandmother the strength of her love by giving her some beautiful flowers. 0 They reached the garden, but paused at the gate, as they were attracted by the sound of a loud voice that came from a poor cottage on the opposite side of the way. "If you cannot pay me," said the voice, "the sooner you go the better. I am not going to lose my rent, I can tell you." "Indeed," replied the trembling voice of a woman, "you slfall not. I have a promise of work, and my husband is getting better. Have patience, and §ou shall lose noth- ing." "Fine talk, mistress; said Ulf man, "but I cannot afford to listen to it. lam not a hard man, or I might take your furniture. As it is, you must go." "Then Heaven help us l'" sobbed the woman, "it will kill My husband." The children looked at each other. They could hear the bitter sobs of the woman. "Could we help them?" said Mary. "Of course not," said. Lena, "we need all we have." Then she went .',. into the garden, leaving Mary puzzled as to what to do. When Lena had chosen some choice flowers, Mary came running in with flushed cheeks. "Oh, Lena," she cried, "I - went to the cottage—l could not help iit—and ' my little gold piece was enough to pay the rent and leave something beside." Neither Lena nor Simon showed any pleasure at what she had done, and poor Mary,felt chilled for want of ! sympathy. As they left the garden they semi : the woman standing at the door of her cottage • with a pot of violet, in her hand. "Will you ' ) take them, young lady?" said the woman. "It is all we can offer in return for your kindness. My husband has tended them through his ill- ' ness, and it will be a comfort to him if you will take them." Mary did not like to deprive the sick man of his treasure, but she saw she would displease him unless she did so. "Lena," said she, "I will give these to grandmother." "Oh, they are only violets," replied Lena. They now went to their grandmother's house, where they found many other telations, who had all brought presents to grandmamma. l'o°r Mary's pot of violets looked very plain an' simple among the many splendid flowers stand- ing on the table. Aunt Jenny, at first, was dis- pleased with Mary. She thought that - Mary had kept the money for her own pleasure. As Lena was too good natured to let Mary lie un- der blame for what she did not deserve, she told Aunt Jenny the tale. Aunt Jenny must thave ayt ogl good-bye, dgrbayned, mhoetrh egrr.anWd mh oe nt h eMr asrayi said, Dt euarp child, I know the history of your gift. A richer present could give me no greater pleasure. To-day Day little Mary has shown her kind heart." As they went home, Mary's little heart was full of content. She was pleased as she remembered her grandmother's words.
From your sincere niece, GLLDYS KNIGHT.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am writing to ask you if I can join the "Children's Corner." I have been away for a very long holiday, and have had a most enjoyable time. Hoping to see my_ name in .the paper as tt new member. I an 15 years of age. Birthday, September 2. I remain, your loving niece, DOROTHY M. OLNEY.
"IT'S THE CAT !" That s Who it is—the cat!

--- - The milk is short; the cream is poor; Who's• fond of milk—well, to be sure, Who steals it? Why, you fiat Who but the cat? It's no one but the cat, Th‘ window broke—not by a ball From Johnny's bat—oh, not at all, Johnny takes care of that, But it's the cat! Sure it's the cat. The clothes were drying at the fire, And some were burnt. Need you inquia Who knocked them down t like that? Who but the cat?

div.p: Leigh provided the loot last Saturday, and as the contest was in the first round of the Lancashire Cup Warrington may be considered to have started auspiciously. The Leigh men have a League match to play at Warrington yet, and I don't suppose they are looking forward to the prospvt. However,there'us time for a few changes before Christmas Day, and then, too, a lot depends on the pudding.

It does not often fall to the lot of a team to score 18 points away from home and still lose. In fact, with all the scoring there has been this season a similar feat has only been performed by one other club, viz., Hull, who scored 19 points against Hunslet's 23 at Hull on 'September Ist. Freak scoring is to be expected under the present rules, but it is almost as surprising to find that in only two matches during the whole of the League contests since September Ist has only one solitary try been scored. I thought the record was held by the Broughton —Warrington match but find that Runcorn won at Leigh by 2 goals 1 try to nil on September 22nd. Leigh have participated in'the making of both records, but tho experience can hardly be gratifying.

The following are some of last week's results, played on ground of first-named• : Bowdon 7, Bebbington 4. Timperley 4, New Brighton Wanderers 0. Oston 4, Brooklands 1. Formby 2, Buyton 1. Bankfield 3, Latchford 3.

According to a watchmaker, thunderstorms , have a bad effect upon ;watches, the mainsprings of which are sometimes broken by the heavy charges, of electricity. "Singularly enough;" he said, "although scores of mainsprings are found •to have collapsed after a heavy storm, I have r•ever met anybody who could give me a scientific explanation of the phenomenon. This ,is probably due to the fact that the injury to ;he twitch is seldom or never attributed by the I owner of it to what I consider to be the true I cause. That atmospheric changes have a notice- able effect on watches is, of course, well known. Thus, in cold weather, the average watch has a tendency to run sluggishly; while in hot weather it is likely to get ahead of the Green- wich time. These effects of the atmosphere would be much more marked but for the fact I that to protect watches against these influences I the balance wheels are made in two pieces, aryl of steel and brass combined. This allows for th ,e contraction caused by atmospheric changes."

div.head: SUNLIGHT AND HEALTH.
div.p: SUNLIGHT AND HEALTH.

It has long been known that sunlight is im- portant to health; the shady side of the street is always more unhealthy than the sunny side. French- physicians treat nen-oas diseases by put- ting the patients under glass roofs, where they are compelled to be in the sun's rays all day long. •Dr. Pease, a physician of San Francisco. has been snaking interesting experiments with the sun's rays as a curative power in lung dis- eases. He has consumptive tendencies himself, and found himself benefited by sptnding an hour or two every day in a photograph gallery, lighted by, a skylight of blue class, and having the walls tinted with blue. Following out the idea suggested by this experience, he' has tested other colours, and finds that purple or light violet has a wonderful sanitary power. All con- sumptives are benefited by living in rooms lighted by violet-coloured glass; and the patient pronounced incurable by eminent physicians, he declares, was completely cured by the use of a red purple light. The sun is the great fountain of light and motion to our world. It will be a curious fact if it is found to be also the most skil- ful physician.

div.head: WATER-FINDING EXPERIMENTS.
div.p: WATER-FINDING EXPERIMENTS.

Some interesting experiments with water- finder's and investigations into their claima have been carried out by Professor Wertheimer, principal of the Merchant Venturers' Technical College, Bristol. In a re.port published in the Tiin ics t was 'stated that the experiinents were divided into six classes: (1) Experiments to find known wells or water channels feeding them; (2) experiments to ascertain -if the motion of a dowser's rod is due to an electrical cause; (3) experiments to find a known underground channel; (4) comparisons of retults obtained by different dowsers on the same spots; (5) experi- ments to discover when water is or is not flow. ing iii an iron pipe; and (6) experiments to fincli gold and silver. In so far as these experiments have gone, Professor Wertheimer , states, I am inclined to believe that the motion of the dowser's rod and the sensations which he experiences are not due to any cause outside • himself. The experiments do not answer definitely the question whether or not dowsers have the power to find water: but i think they shew (a) that experienced dowsers did not give the same indications in the same place, and (b) that the movements of their rods were, in several of the experiments described duo purely to subjective causes,

div.head: TO PURIFY DRINKING. WATER.
div.p: TO PURIFY DRINKING. WATER.

To purify drinking-water, M. Lambert pro- poses, in the British and Colonial Druggist, to add 6cgms. of permanganate of potash to each litre. This should be left ten minutes, after Itftich lOcgms. of manganous sulphate should be added. This precipitates all germs and im- purities to the bottom of the kvessel. Carefully decanted this will give "water not containing a single microbe, limpid, colourless, of pleasant taste, and even richer in oxygen than ordinary water."

FUTURE OF THE • SUN'S ACTIVITY. Professor T. J. J. See has Announced a new , law of heat accumulation, in an article in the Atlantic Monthly, by virtue of which he predicts that the future of the sun's activity will be three times BA great as that of ,the past, thus overturning the prevailing astronomical theory. Calculations made by Professor See prove the • existence of a law applying to the life of every sun and star, 'acting to ' which the heat steadily , increases, While the body is gaseous, and then ' slowly dies down by similar cooling, when con- • solidation sets in and the light begins to wane.

THE HARVEST MOON. I As the sun at the autumn equinox crosses the equator at its descending node,' and moves southward, the duration of daylight lessens more rapidly than at any other period, says a contem- porary. On the other hand, the moon crosses tlu equator at its ascending node, and comes northward, as a result of which the duration of moonlight is at its maximum, and generously compensates for the early withdrawal of the brighter luminary; the small angle between the moon's path and the ecliptic causing moonrise to occur for several nights in succession at nearly the same hour and before twilight has ended.

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. J. MORTON.—Owing to the pressure of election news this week we are regretfully compelled to hold over your letter in reply to " Gasworker."—En. " Ex."

Baptist Church Finances. Sir,—Referring to correspondence that has appeared in your columns rs Baptist Church Finances, I beg to say that we have now submitted our church and school accounts to Mr. Edwin Bradshaw, chartered accountant, and I herewith enlose his report from which it will be seen that the deficit on the church (or general account) at June 30th, 1906, was £54 4s. 61,d. This proves that we were quite right in stating that we had a deficit in our church finances of £5O, as we were referring only to the general account.—Yours truly E. div.head: Tree Planting at Stockton Heath.
div.p: Tree Planting at Stockton Heath.

Sir,—With respect to the recent Parish Council meeting at Stockton Heath of which we have heard so much will you kindly allow me to refer to a statement by one of the members at that meeting viz. :—That he had never been opposed to the planting of trees in Daskell-street or Heath-street. Why sir, it is well- known that so great was his opposition to the trees in Heath-street that a petition was drawn up and presented to the Committee, by the inhabitants of that street, against the removal of the trees. As to Daskell-street if any of your readers will look up the Warrington papers when the agitation was on—one of which is now before me—they will see that he pleaded at Dutton for their iemoval. I leave the consideration of the two statements to your readers.
TRUTH.

Considerable interest centred in the public meeting held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Thurs- day evening under the auspices of the Progressive Lab- our League. The principal speaker was Mr. Havelock Wilson, M.P. for Middlesborough who is well-known for his strenuous work on behalf of the Seamen's and Firemen's Union and against whom the Shipping Federation (the powerful organization of the ship- owners) has recently enforced a judgment of long- standing, evidently with the intention of causing him to become bankrupt and thus lose his seat in Parlia- ment. Notwithstanding counter-attractions, there was a good attendance. Mr. George Walker presided and was supported on the platform by Mr. Havelock Wilson, M.P., Mr. Joseph Howes. Messrs. W. Furness, S. Wright, J. Elwell and J. Morton (secretary of the League.) The CHAIRMAN, after referring to the great triumph gained at the last election, said the Unionist party detested democracy, they disliked the growing power of the Labour party, and they were totally opposed to religious equality. Sound Liberals were pleased with the return to power of a number of Labour men, for they contended that the men who could best legislate for the majority were those who came into personal contact with them and had had their training in Corporations, Friendly and Co-operative Societies, and Trade Unions. (Applause.) They were sorry that there should be any signs of dissension and that such good old horses as John Burns, Mr. Maddison and Mr. Have- lock Wilson,whom he claimed were thoroughly qualified to represent the workers and to voice their claims, should seem to suffer any degree of slighting. With regard to Mr. Havelock Wilson, his work had been so strenuous and far-reaching as to gain the disapprobation , of the Shipping Federation. The reason was that he had discovered some of the gross injustices that had been paramont in the shipping world, and seamen in particular owed him a debt of gratitude. (Applause). THE ELECTIONS.

Mr. MORTON in a short address with reference to the November elections, appealed to his hearers to support Councillor Barton in Whitecross Ward, Mr. Halliwell In St. Austin's Ward, Councillor Maginn in St. John's • Ward, and himself in Bewsey Ward. MR. HAVELOCK WILSON'S SPEECH. WHAT HE HAS HAD TO CONTEND WITH.

Mr. HAVELOCK WILSON, M.P., who was welcomed with great cordiality, said he had come there not to talk on behalf of himself but to explain some- thing of the trials and difficulties which surrounded the lives of the sea-faring men of this country. It was, he , contended, the duty of the nation to afford seameu even greater protection than was given to the men on shore who had always got the law courts or other remedies , close ist hand. He appealed more particularly on behalf , of the men who were married and had wives and chil- dren. He had had twenty-six years' hard fighting for the seamen. Some of his critics of the Independent Labour Party had said that the seamen ought to be the most J strongly-organized body of men in the world. He J: had made an offer to those would-be Labour leaders that if they imagined that they could , organize the seamen better than he could, he was quite prepared to stand down and give them a ; chance. Moreover, if they succeeded in accomplishing what he had not been able to accomplish he would be prepared to vacate his seat in Parliament and give them J the pleasure of representing that particular class of workers. Mr. Wilson then dealt at some length with the difficulties of organizing seamen, pointing out that ,the sea-faring population included all nationalities. 'Over 60,000 Lascars and Chinamen were employed lin the mercantile marine and the remainder included •evee3o,ooo foreigners, comprising 13 or 14 nationalities. 'Nearly 50 per cent. of the seamen had no settled homes. ,For fifteen years the Seamen's Union had had to fight the strongest combination of capital in the country— the Shipping Federation—which represented the 'majority of the shipowners and was worth 130 millions •of money. He did not object to a combination of .employers, for he believed that with perfect combina- tion on both sides they need have no fear of strikes for they would disappear and commonsense would prevail with masters and men. The shipowners, however, had gone beyond that and they had established in overy port offices where every man who was engaged on ship must practically declare himself to be a non- unionist. (" Shame.") If the officials had the slightest enspicion that an applicant for work was a Union man he would get a chance of employment when they could pat get aeyone else. •It cost the Shipping Federation something.iike £lO,OOO a year to run the organization ft order,to keep the Seaman's Union down. In 1890 they started a system of persecution against himself and other official:7,, and for over six years employed a number of men, some Lf whom had at that time been in gaol and others had been thece since—he met one the other week who had just come out after doing three years and who was a preminent man amongst them—and their business was to follow him round the country circu- lating libellous,pamphlets and challenging him to take them into the law courts. The object was to harra.ss him, to keep kiln in the Courts spending time and money, and thus impoverish the funds of the Union and himself. Mr. Wilson referred to the Glasgow strike which resulted in his being proceeded against by the Shipping Federaeion in respect of a leaflet which he had not signed and which was issued in his absence. A verdict for £340 and costs was obtained against him and elthongh it was over six years since the action was tried, he never heard anything farther about it until he was returned to Parliament and had made a speech or two in the House and announced on the public platform what he intended to do in the way of shipping legislation. Then the wealthy Shipping Federation suddenly discovered that be owed them £B4O and made a demand that be should "brass up" at once. The main object of the Federation was to close his mouth in the House of Common's when he was advocating the cause of the seamen. He was satisfied that the majority .of ship owners repadiated the business with scorn. It was only a few of the meanest Jhucksters amongst them who were really responsible for this contemptible trick. Wilson then referred to his successful effort to get the Workmen's Compensation Aet. extended to include seamen and said that thanks to the present Govern- ment he had been able to isecomplish almost the work of a life time. He also dealt with the principal clauses which he had had incorporated in the Merchants' shipping Bill. One was that every seaman should have a decent scale of pro- visione, and Mr. Wilson was able to demonstrate to his nedience from personal experience how sorely needed this wee. Continuing, he alleged that men had in the past been driven out of ships by harsh treatment, for no other puepose than that the money they loft behind should be confiscated by the shiponmers.He did not bring a charge of that kind against ship owners generally— such practices were confined to a very small eection— but it was necessary that they should have the law strengthened to protect the men, even if only one ship- owner was involved. In future when a man deserted a ship and left money behind, the owner - allowed any expenses to which he le had been put by obtaininget substitute, ance should be handed to the State. User to ask the State that the money thus hould be deboted to the provision of old for saiiara. (Applause). Mr. Wilson other serious grievances under which sea- chiding lack of proper accommodation, . that sailors had actually been impris- Inc to run tbe blockade during the Russo- Continuing M.-. lYi/eton said he had had '

enough litigation to be a barrister five times I over. (Laughter). During the past two years he had had three cases in the House of Lords and one was still waiting to be disposed of. He had four cases running in the Court of Appeal and fifteen in the High Courts. He claimed that he was doing a public work hat that the Shipping Federation did not fight him fairly. When the bankruptcy proceedings were instituted he received a telegram from a sailor offering to place LW—the savings of a life-time—at his dis- posal. (Applause.) He believed he had public opinion and support on his side. (Applause.) MR. CROSFIELD'S DONATION.

Mr. HowEs said a number of workingmen volunteered to collect in their works on Mr. Wilson's behalf and so far the returns had been extremely handsome. (Applause.) Mr. A. H. Crosfleld, M.P., bad written as follows to Kr. Barnes, the president of the League :—" Beacon Hotel,Crowborough. Dear Sir,—Will you kindly tell Mr. Havelock Wilson and the members of the Progressive Labour League what a grievous disappointment it is to me that circumstances prevent me attending your meeting to-morrow night. I have, as it chances, had a good deal on my hands since Parliament rose and have been ordered to take a fortnight's rest and quiet in the country here before we meet again at Westminster on the 23rd. I ara told a subscription will be made to-morrow night on behalf of Mr. Havelock Wilson. If that is so will you kindly add the enclosed contribution to it. Mr. Wilson's splendid services on behalf of our seamen are known to all and in the House of Commons he is deeply respected as one of those who, without wasting time seeking chimerical short cuts to Utopia, work strenuously for what is practicable and possible and just in the interests of labour. lam sure your meeting to-morrow night will be a great success and I only wish I might be present at it." Mr. Crosfield enclosed a cheque for ten guineas. (Applause.) Mr. Howes moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Wilson and expressed the hope that he would soon revisit Warring- ton. (Applause). CRITICISM OF THE TRADES COUNCIL. Mr. S. WRIGHT 'seconded. He said that not long ago the question of Mr. Wilson's position came before the Trades and Labour Council and as an old trade unionist and one who had been con- nected with the Trades Council many years and had occupied the presidency and vice-presidency, he felt exasperated at the result of their deliberations on the subject. It had always been the practice when he was connected with the Trades Council that when a member of a trade organization had been victimised in any way they snould make it their first duty to help him. (Applause). It could not be on account of Mr. Wilson's trade unionism that the Trades Council did not respond to the appeal, for if any were not satisfied with the work he had done, he (Mr. Wright) considered they were no friends of trade unionists. He would appeal to trade unionists to attend their Union meetings and see that those organizations were conducted on trade Cnion lines, and that their funds were used only for Trade Union pur- poses. He hoped the present action of the Trades Council would be a lesson to the Trade unionists of ‘Varrington, and that they would see that their work was not prostituted in the way it had been in this town. (Applause). The motion was heartily carried. Mr. HAVELOCK WILSON in responding said he was a trade unionist and he ventured to say, without boasting, that it all the Independent Labour Party men were got together from all ends of the country, he could prove that he had done more fighting for Labour in one year than the whole lot of them had done in a lifetime. What was more, he had suffered for the cause. (Applause.) As a matter of fact many Independent Labour Party men helped him in the fight, but it was the extreme Keir Hardieites who opposed him. He had received a letter from a Unionist ex-candidate sympathising with him and enclosing a donation. Yet the Independent Labour Party of Warrington moved that] the appeal should lie on the table. They could not say a word against his trade unionism or his fighting for Labour.All they could say was that he stood up for Liberalism and Labour. Trade unionism was being attacked in this fight and the Independent Labour Party of Warrington were such good trade unionists that they delined to assist(A voice: They are hypocrites). He did not know about being hypocrites, but they were not above lending a hand to the free labour gang that he was fighting. They moved that the letter should lie on the table so that the workingmen of Warrington should be prevented from subscribing and so that the greatest free labour organization in the country should defeat a trade unionist. That was the policy of the Independent Labour Party of Warrington. He hoped the workingmen trade unionists of Warring- ton would remember them and when they came on a public platform it would be just as well that a few questions should be asked them as to whether they believed in trade unionism or free labour. (Applause.) A vote of thanks to the Chairman, proposed by Mr. HAVELOCK WitsoN,M.P.,and seconded by Mr. ELWELL, concluded the meeting.

Independent Order of Oddfellows (Manchester Unity). On Saturday the quarterly meeting of the Warring- ton District was held at the Pelican Hotel. 8..0. T. P. Bradshaw, Prov. Grand Master, presided and was supported by Bros. W. Holbrook, Prov. Deputy Grand Master,Frank Webster, Prov. C. S-.,and T. Wadsworth, District Treasurer, together with the full number of delegates. The accounts for the past quarter were read and passed and disclosed a gain to the Funeral Fund on the quarter of £lO3 Os. alter paying funeral benefits amounting to £OO. During the quarter 17 members were initiated, 20 members had lapsed and 7 members had died. The strength of the District was 1038. The District Funeral Fund amounted to £2,760 4s. 11(1. P.G. W. Dennett gave a report of the proceedings of the Lancashjre and adjacent Dis- trict Conference held at Burnley on 15th September and a vote of thanks was accorded to him. It was unanimously resolved that the sum of £2l be given to the Warrington Infirmary Extension Fund and that a sum of £5 be voted to the Warrington and District Nursing Association. It was 3ecided that the District be represented at the next A.M.C. at Folkestone and the following nominations were received: -Prov. D.G.M. William Holbrook, Prov. C. S. Frank Webster, P.P.G.M. Ellis R. Clare, P.P.G.M. James 11(1a8sey, P.G. Walter Knowles and PG. John A. Wright. Prov. D.G.M. William Holbrook was nominated for the position of Prov. Grand Master. The following nominations were received for the position of Prov. D.G. Master : P.G. Lot Brooks, P.G. George F. Free- man and P.G. Albert E Burdett. The meeting closed with a hearty vote of thanks to Prov. G.M. Bradshaw for presiding.
