div.head: Examiner, Saturday, October 20, 1906.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, October 20, 1906.
NON-TRADERS' MEETINGS.
The Personnel of the Council.
CRITICISM OF THE MAYOR.

'The Non-Trading Association has during the week held two public meetings in connection with the forth- coming municipal elections. The first,which was in sup- port of the candidature of Councillor Elijah Cunnington (Liberal Non-Trader) in Orford Ward, was hold in Silver-street schools on Tuesday evening. Eller° was a fair attendance presided over by Mr. James Dodds who was supported by Mr. Robert Cameron, M.P.,Councillors Pemberton and Skelland, and the candidate. MR. DODDS AND THE PERSONNEL OF THE COUNCIL.

The CHAIRMAN, in opening the meeting, said Coun- cillor Cunnington had for some months past faithfully served the best interests of their town in the Council Chamber. They had found that he had got that back bone and determination which' were neler so much needed as at that moment in that assembly, and he had been loyal to the principle for which the Non-Trading Association was formed, and which had now the sympathy and support of all that was best in the public sentiment of Warrington. (Applause). Less than a year ago the Conservative and the Liberal candidates for their representation in Parliament both uncondition- ally accepted

div.head: UNDERLYING PRINCIPLE
div.p: THE UNDERLYING PRINCIPLE

- of the movement. Their questions were put to Mr. Pierpoint and to Mr. Crosfield as follows :—"I. Are you of opinion' that no representative elected to any public body should derive pecuniary profit, either 1 directly or indirectly, by reason of his membership of such public body ; and if so-2. Would you vote for a Bill in Parliament which would make it illegal for mem- bers of County, Borough and District Councils to trade with the Council of which they are members, whether through limited companies or otherwise." Both their pre- sent member and Mr. Pierpoint answered those questions to their entire satisfaction, and he was satisfied that at that moment the great majority of the ratepayers, and a large majority of the members of the Council would do the same. If that were so he might be asked "Why is the position of the Non-Trading councillors so intolerable in the Council and on committees?" It was because the leading members of the party were so zealous for the ratepayers' interests, so determined that business should be satisfactorily done, and that nothing should be taken for granted on the more assurance of chairmen or of the officials, that, in fact, the aldermen and the officials should not, as had bean too often the , case, usurp the positions of the elbcted representatives of the ratepayers. Naturally those councillors who were unwilling to take the trouble to do their own work were annoyed and incensed when they found men like Councillor Pemberton and Councillor Lord take the trouble which they would not take, and getting at facts of vital importance to the ratepayers. • He (the chair- man) need only refer to the Lawson Contract, and to the unsatisfactory way in which properties had been bought and dealt with to indicate the importance of the work their men had done, and to account for the way in which they had been treated in consequence of their determination to get at the bottom of things. (Aprlause). In regard to

Tali LAWSON CONTRACT, would the ratepayers have ever known the facts of that business and that the extras on a contract of £21,000 , were now put down at about £50,000? 'Would they base believed that but for Councillor Pemberton's heroic pluck and determination the larger part of that immense claim would probably have been paid without much question? (Applause.) He considered it seri- ously wrong that where an elected representative was striving to save the ratepayers' pockets, he should have the virulent opposition of those who ought to have been working with him, but who allowed their personal dis- likes and jealousies to turn them from their duty. The responsibility for the scenes in the Council did not lie at the door of the Non-trading members.lt was time it was said,and he was going to say it—the fault was, and had been for three years past,with the chs.ir.A president,or a chairman, or a mayor, should excerise the duties of his position with absolute impartiality. He should know no party, show no temper' and treat his opponents as if they were his friends. He should hold an even hand and intervene as seldom as possible in the proceedings and then only with firmness and dignity. (Hear, hear.) The

div.head: bIGNITY OF THE MAYORALTY
div.p: bIGNITY OF THE MAYORALTY

had not been maintained during the pass three years. He said that with great regret, as he was one of those who waited upon and prevailed upon Alderman Bolton to accept the position, and he knew he had certain good qualities. He observed a suggestion had been made that the three associations of Warrington ratepayers, the Non-traders, the Property Owners,and the Tradesmen might combine on the one subject of supplying the town with a Council they could trust and respect. On behalf of the Non- trading Association, he was in a position to say that they were prepared to work with the other associations named for the object in view,provided that their simple platform was accepted, namely that no member sent to the Council should derive profit in any way by reason of such membership. Mr. Cunnington stood on that plat- form. He knew of the immense financial loss to the ratepayers and the demoralization of aldermen, coun- cillors and officials resulting from the immoral dealings now happily driven under if not entirely swept away, and he knew of the existence of a lurking desire in the hearts of some of those he had referred to, to bring back the bad old days when the ratepayers' money was running away like water, and things were made so pleasant all round. (Applause). He observed also, that Mr. Cunnington was a Liberal Non-trader, Personally, , he (the Chairman) did not approve of the INTRODUCTION OF NATIONAL PARTY POLITICS into municipal contests. He agreed with President Roosevelt when he said that "The worst evils that affect our local government arise from, and are the inevitable result of mixing up city affairs with the party politics of the nation and of the state. The lines 1 upon which national parties divide have no necessary connection with the business of a town ; such connec- tion opens the way to countless schemes of public plunder and civic corruption." (Applause.) The mixing up of town affairs with the party politics of the nation had been carried to a fine art in Warrington. The same machinery had worked both, and the result had not only been seen in Wallington, but was known throughout the country. If he were a candidate ho should stand as he had done before, entirely apart from party. (Applause.) What was wanted was that a man should be honest, fearless and capable, and not! that he should be either blue, red or green ' • er Tory, , Liberal or Labour. (Applause.) flowerer, he knew that Mr. Cannin.gton was first of all for purity and economy with efficiency, and there never was a time when the strictest economy was more necessary. Here were some figures which should make them all pause. The Imperial expenditure per head of the population in this country for the year 1881-2 was £2 7s. Gd. and for the year 1902-3 £3 3s. Bd. per head of the population, or an increase of 38 per cent. The local expenditure per load of population for the year 1881-2 was £1 17s. 10d. and for the year 1902-3 £3 Ils. 11d. per head of the population, an increase of DO per cent. Surely these were startling figures, Ivod should induce every rate- payer to consider well as to how he voted and whether his bounden duty was not to support the Non-traders, who had brought down the Warrington capital expendi- ture so remarkably, and, apart from the special charges for education, had so sensibly reduced the rates of the town. (Applause). COUNCILLOR PENIBERTON PROTESTS AGAINST SECRECY. THE PROPERTY PURCHASING QUESTION.

Councillor PEMBERTON, introduced by the Chairman as "the best man in the Town Council, said that any work he had done he had been pleased to do for the ratepayers, and all he wanted was the voters to send the Non-traders additional councillors, and to return those now before the electors. One of the greatest difficul- ties in public life was to get one's views put before the members of the Council. Unfortunately there were a select few who knew direct from the officials what business was coming before the Council. There were a few who, like the Non-traders, ferreted these things out for themselves with great trouble. But such trouble ought not to be put upon any councillor. The business of the Corporation ought to be transacted so that the minute details which could be reasonably expected were , placed before the members of a committee. One of the I greatest difficulties they had to contend against was the secrezy with ..thich the business of the public was carried on in the town. That was mainly owing to ' certain officials and aldermen. They must not think lte was running down all the officials, as they had in some of the subordinate ones some of the finest officials any Corporation had in England. (Applause). Certain officials in high places were, however, altogether wrong and instead of doing the work straight and above board for the whole of the members they only consulted certain old members and aldermen. What he wanted was open- ness. If matters were straight why cover everything up ? (Hear, hear.) Alluding to the purchase of Colonel Edelsten's property, Councillor Pemberton said that question had been on the carpet for two years but he rever knew anything about it until he became a member of the Street Improvement Committee. He was quite as ignorant about it as any other ratepayer was. He believed that when a committee got the refusal of property at a certain price the matter ought to come before the Council. Many people said that the Non- Traders were attacking the officials, but was there any- one in Warrington who could tell him how they were going to carry on the business of the town and expose' anything that was wrong unless they got across with the officials ? They got across an official if they as councillors exposed anything he had done by a slip, purposely, or in other ways. (Applause.) He could have a good name in the Council if he wished. .(Laugh- ter.) He could be very friendly with the officials. He knew how to do it. In 12 months if he laid himself out

That would be pleasanter to him, he admitted, but would it be looking after the interests of the ratevapers? 1 (Applause.) He distinctly denied that the Non-Traders i were opposing the Labour party. As that gentleman ran away, he (gr. Dodds) withdrew in favour of the Labour candi- date in Bewsey Ward. He felt he could do as much good for the cause outside the Council as in it. ("No.") If, however, it was found absolutely necessary that he should go into the Council he was prepared to go. (Applause.) He had made some sacrifices for the cause. (Hear, hear.) It was said some people had made for- tunes; he was more likply to lose one. He was pre- pared to go on spending money and to fight for this cause in Warrington because he knew it was vital to the interests of the workingmen of the town that the extrava- gant government which had threatened the town with bankruptcy should be swept away. (Applause.) gr. Dodds contended that the effect of trading by members of the Council with the Corporation was to demoralize the officials.

That was what the Non-Traders objected to. They ojected to being made the detectives of the Corporation. (Hear hear.) If the other men had not the time, inclination or ability to go into matters for themselves they had no right to be on the Council. (Hear, hear.) If the ratepayers were going to illow that sort of thing to continue there was no telling what expense the Council might not be landed into. (Applause.) He thought the time had arrived when Air. leading men of the town shinild support them on the Council and Mr. Dodds was just the man to help them. They wanted men in the Council who had the courage to vote as they believed to be in the beat interests of the ratepayers and not men like some of the present members of the Council, who would not vote until they were given the lead. Referring to the BIRTLES' PROPERTY Councillor Lord said they had no quarrel with Mr. Birtl es or with Mr. Garnett. The people they quarrelled with were the people in the Town Hall who had not looked after the interests of the ratepayers and who had not done as well for the town as they might have done. (Hear, hear.) The motion was put to the meeting and unanimously and heartily carried. Con- tinuing he said the political compact had resulted in the corruption and irregularities in the Corporation and until the party system was smashed they could never do anything and would not get pure government. They did not want men in the Council because they called themselves Liberals or anything else. They wanted the men who were honest, good business men, fearless and able to do the work. If he was beaten in the fight he would not be disgraced, but he thought that if they ' put their case fairly before the ratepayers the public would see that it was absolutely the best for the interests of the ratepayers and absolutely above the programme of the party men. Councillor DICKINSON said he had had a conversation with Mr. Hill who said that if they insisted upon running Mr. Walker he would retire in favour of Coun- cillor Wilson. That did not appear as though he would support the Non-Traders. There were too many men in the Council who promised to support the Non-Traders in order to secure their help at election times and who when they got in the Council turned round upon the Non-Traders. (Applause.) Alderman PIERPOINT said he was not present as a member of the Non-Trading Association. He was there as an admirer of the action taken by the Association and so far as his influence could go and so long as the Association continued in the line of action which it had followed in the past so long would he give them all the help which he could. A great deal was said about the composition of the Non- Trading party. Mr. Pemberton was a double-dyed blackguard," Councillor Lord was described in almost similar terms and in a smaller degree the other mem- bers were included. He had alwtts said Coun- cillor Pemberton was somewhat of a diamond in the rough but he had always found him to be an honest man. No man in public life in War- ington had had to stand the same amount of slanging and libellous statements as Councillor Pemberton, but, fortunately, he had a skin as thick as a three-inch board, and instead of being harmed, seemed to improve under the treatment. That he (Councillor Pember- ton) was honest was proved by the manner in which he received the treatment meted out to him. Anyone who was not honest would not have stood the treatment for a moment. lie (Alderman Pierpoint) would not under any conditions countenance and &ippon the Non-Traders unless he was satisfied that the objects which they had in view were the best for the town. They had wisely decided to accept Mr. Dodds as their candidate in Latchford Ward and for his part he would do all ho possibly could to support his candidature—(applause)—and he hoped they would carry the tight to a successful issue. (Applause.) Mr. ALFRED HULME in a humorous speech urged the necessity of the Non-Trading party being strengthened by sending such excellent men as Mr. Dodds to the Council. (Applause). Mr. ROBERT CAMERON, M.P., also congratulated the meeting upon their selection of a candidate. Mr. Dodds was a good business man, honourable minded, just and true and a man who could rise above party politics and above private intorests. (Applause). Unless the democracy of the town would take mere of their privi- leges they would soon sink to the level of New York or Chicago. England must live higher than that and they must have honest men to represent them and legislate , for them. (Applause). Mr. DODDS explained his reason for retiring from the Council when he was returned at the outset of their agitation and assured his hearers that if elected in the present contest he would serve the full term of the office. (Applause.) A member of the audience risked why the Non-traders had singled out Councillor Wilson as the man to attack on the question of the payment of Mayor's auditor? Why had they not attacked a wealthier man? Mr. DODDS Said that when the Non-Trading agitation started, Mr. Jolley was the Mayor's auditor, and be was defeated at the first election which followed the commencement of the campaign. Since then Alder- man Frfirclough had filled the officeand had not received the fee. Couecillor Wilson was the first to receive the fee since then and therefore that was the first oppor- tunity they had had of testing the matter. He was not anxious to put Councillor Wilson to any legal costs becaese he thought it would be hard upon him. If a man who was in a position to fight accepted the fee, he would be fought. (Applause.) Mr. S. KEN YON said that a week ago Mr. Dodds had not the slightest idea of contesting Latchford Ward and it was a great personal sacrifice for him to do so, and he hoped they would return Mr. Dodds by a large majority. Mr. Dodds was the splendid champion of a noble cause,for good government and disinterestedness in public life.He did not like to speak of religion,but that was Christianity reduced to practice, and yet they had been told that Non-Traders were actuated by animus and were bringing the town into disrepute. It was not the Non-Traders but the irregularities of the town that had disgraced the town. (Applause). Mr. DODDS thanked the meeting for selecting him as the candidate and the proceedings ended.

div.head: Tile Position in Latchford Ward. Mr. James Dodds to Stand.
div.p: Tile Position in Latchford Ward. Mr. James Dodds to Stand.

Since our last issue the position in Latchford Ward has undergone a change. As we announcecl,Mr. Edward Walker had agreed to uphold the Non-Trading standard in opposition to Councillor Wilson but ill-health has caused his withdrawal from the contest. A meeting was held in St. James school on Thursday night, to consider the situation and in response to the unanimous wish of a large audience Mr. James Dodds promised to fight on behalf of the party with which he has been so closely identified. The chair was occupied by Mr. Dodds who was supported by Mr. Robert Camerson, Alderman Pierpoint, Councillors Skelland, Pemberton, Lord, Benson and Dickinson,and Messrs.S. Kenyon, R. Isherwood, and A. Hulme. At the outset Mr. Dodds said Mr. Walker's medical attendant had forbidden him to stand and had said he would not speak for Mr. Walker living through the election if he went on with it. As they knew the Non- Traders were bound to fight the ward. (Hear, hear.) In a letter which he wrote to the Press a few weeks ago he said that on account of Councillor Wilson having accepted £3O as Mayor's auditor they were, in view of their principles bound to fight him, and try and turn him out of the Council. (Hear, hear). 'He said that no man in the position of Councillor Wilson who received £3O a year could be the independent representative of the ratepayers, but that he was absolutely at the co in- mond of the people who gave blue the position and of the party will which he(Counoillor Wilson )was assoc ted who would at once threaten to stop the piyment if he did not doss he was told. A mania COUNCILLOR WILSON'S POSITION.

could not be a satisfactory representative of the rate- payers. (Mr. Dodds) intended at the time to get a Judge's opinion as to the legality of the payment. but found that the law's delay, which was proverbial, was such that the election was on them before they could put the law in motion. He had no personal feeling against Mr. Wilson. Quite the contrary but he felt that the issue should 'be settled once and for all. The law—the Municipal Cor- porations Act—said as distinctly as possible that no man who was a meraber of a Town Council or any public body should receive, directly or indirectly,any profit to the smallest amount as a result of his member- ship of that body. In that case they had a member of the Town Council receiving .£3O and if that was not a violation of the Act he did not know what was. The Non-Traders did not stop at the law. They raid it was morally wrong that a man, under any circumstances, even legally, should receive any kind of pay whilst a member of is public body. (Applause). That was what they said when they started their agita- tion five years ago, at which time it was possible to count on the fingers of two hands the members of the Council who were not receiving profit, directly or indirectly, in connection with the position they held. The first election fought on their principles they won, and since then they found that their position had been gradually strengthened in the Council, not so much by pew members as by men who had voted with them and accepted their principles, so that if a vote was now taken on the question as to whether a man should make anything from his position their principles would be carried by a considerable majority. But they did not find that enough. They had seen the result of the wrongdoings when men were using their public position for their private ends,also in the Lawson contract and the purchasing of property without the sanction of the Council, and the borrowing o money before the sanction of the Local Government Board had been obtained. They found all that, even though their main principle had been carried. They said those things were wrong and wanted stopping and they had been working to bring that about. (Applause.) They knew what Councillor Pemberton had been doing and how he had been treated by the Mayor and two or three of the men who pulled the party strings on either side and they felt that the ratepayers ought to send further men to help them to fight

THE BATTLE OF THE PEOPLE. in the Council. (Applause.) In Latchford Ward they had a Tory candichte whom they had pledged them- selves to ileht,and Mr. Hill. Mr. Hill, who was spoken of as the Liberal candidate for the ward came to him by arrangement on Wednesday and assured him that he was a thorough Non-Trader ; that he was a Non- Trader before he was a Liberal. He had never seen Mr. Hill before and he accepted his word that he meant to be an adherent of their party,but the other members of the Non-Trading Association thought that particular con- test was so important to the interests they had at heart that it would be better to have a candidate absolutely their own, who would not be bound in any way to any other party. He believed that party politics

div.head: ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE ELECTIONS.

There have been some important changes during the week \in the position of affairs relating to the November elections, but anything like an all-round fight seems improbable at the time of writing. Four wards only will, so far as is yet known, be contested on November Ist, and these four are St. Austin's, St, John's, Latchford, and Orford. One contest is additional to those announced last week, Mr. James Halliwell having consented to stand as the Liberal candidate for St. Austin's Ward against Councillor Ashcroft, Non-Trader. Owing to illness, Mr. E. Walker has been compelled to with- draw from the contest, in Latchford Ward, and his place has been taken by Mr. James Dodds. In Orford Ward, matters have been simplified by the withdrawal of Mr. W. M. Sloane, thus leaving only two candidates in the field.

Nominations for the various candidates have to be handed in at the Town Hall before five o'clock on Wednesday next. Already papers on behalf of Coun- cillor Wilson, Councillor Sankey, Mr. W. Pooh, and Mr. J. J. Neild have been handed in. The following is a list of the probable candidates to date: Town Hall Ward Coun. Lord C.-T.) Bewsey Ward llr. J. Morton (L) Whitecross Coun. T. Barton (L.) St. Austin's Coun. T. H. Ashcroft (N.-T.) Mr. J. Halliwell (L.) St. John's. Coon. J. Maginn (L) Mr. T. S. Steel (C.) Latchford Coon. W. J. Wilson (C.) Mr. J. Hughes Hill (L.) Mr. J. Dodds (N.-T.) Fairfield Mr. J. J. Nield (C.) Howley Coun. J. Sankey (C.) Orford Coon. Fl. Cunnington (L.N.-T.) Mr. W. rook (Lab.)

LATCHFORD WARD. Probably the most interesting fight will be in Latch- ford Ward, where the last few days have brought interesting developments. At present it seems likely that the fight will be a three-cornered one, bat the real struggle in any case will be between Councillo: Wilson and gr. James Dodds. Oar renders will recollect that at the time of the payment to Councillor Wilson of £3O as Mayor's Auditor's fee, Mr. Dodds wrote to the press challenging the legality of the payment and protesting against Councillor Wilson thus receiving remuneration from the Borough Funds while a member of the Council Mr. Dodds also promised that the matter should be con- tested before the electors in November, and now that Mr. E. Walker has had to give up the fight Mr. Dodds has come forward to personally champion the cause he sspouses. In a powerful address, which we print on our front page, Mr. Dodds re-iterates and emphasizes his protest against the position Councillor Wilson has allowed himself to be placed in,at the same time object- ing strongly to party representation. We have no doubt that he will win the day. Ho fights the battle solely in the public interest and is unquestionably the man for the ward in which, by the way, he has a considerable financial stake at the Manor Tannery (Parkinsons Limited).

Mr. Dodds' first nomination paper contains the names of Alderman Pierpoint, proposer ; Rev. J. F. Matthews, seconder : and Messrs. John Lunt, J.H. Hackney, John Strange, William Strange, W. Rosebottom, C. H. Bryant, G. H. Cliff°, and Joseph Boardman, assenters. It is reported that Mr. Hill, who accepted an invita- tion to stand in the Liberal interest will withdraw rather than fight a three-cornered battle. ST. JOHN'S WARD.

The contest is almost equally interesting in St. John's Ward. Here Councillor John Maginn,the sitting member is opposed by Mr. T. S. Steel, who would have been, better placed in Fairfield or Howley Wards. Councillor Maginn has been a very useful mem- ber of the Council since his memorable elec- tion three years ago, and in many ways he has proved his capacity and independence. in his address, which we print in this issue, Mr. Maginn makes a strong point of not being the nominee of any party, political, religious, or social, and like Mr. Dodds he expresses disapproval of the introduction of party politics into , municipal affairs. Mr. Magian also draws attention to the improved state of the streets in the Ward, and the reduction of the rates and the price of gas since his election. These are matters which have always claimed Mr. Maginn's earnest attention, and we have no doubt will continue to do so when he has disposed of Mr. Steel. He also advocates once again the erection of a bridge fromHowley into Victoria Park,and the develop- ment of that estate so that it shall be a profit to the town and its inhabitants. , Councillor Maginn's nomination is strongly supported by Mr. S. Wright, Mr. E. J. Guest, Alderman Forshaw, Councillor Dr. Joseph, Alderman Pierpoint, Councillor Wilkinson, Councillor Lord, Councillor Clegg, Mr. J. W. Hayward and Mr. L. Greening. ST. AUSTIN'S WARD. There should be a good fight here, where Mr. J. Halliwell, a well-known Liberal, challenges Councillor Ashcroft, one of the Non-Trading stalwarts. It is a pity, from the public point of view, that a Liberal and Non-Trader are in opposition here. They ought to be united. Mr. Ashcroft is understood to be a Conserva- tive in pqlitics, hence the opposition. His oppone at, we believe, also has strong Non-Trading sympathies. so the choice of the electors may very probably be narrowly divided.

div.head: ORFORD WARD.
div.p: ORFORD WARD.

In this Ward there is anotho complication of interests, for Councillor Cuaningtou (Non-Trader) is opposed by Hr. W. Pook, a Labour nominee. The Non-Traders have always shown a sympathy with the aims of the Labour representatives, and we should imagine that the result of the contest will prove Mr. Pook's intervention to have been unwise.

div.head: EXCELSIOR BAZAAR.
div.p: EXCELSIOR BAZAAR.
BUCKLEY-STREET METHODIST FREE CHURCH.

" Excelsior " is the title which the members of Buckley-street Methodist Free Church have chosen for their three days' bazaar which was opened in the Co-operative Hall, Winwick-street, on Thursday after- noon. The selection is a very appropriate one for, in spite of many discouragements, the workers have been undaunted and, although a great measure of success has crowned their efforts, they are persevering for still higher results. The object of the present enter- prise is to liquidate the debt of £175 on the church and to provide Bibles and Testaments which are urgently needed. It is hoped to raise about :E2OO and the enthusiasm which has been displayed in the cause augurs well for the realization of this laudable ambition. The bazaar hand book contains a most interesting history of the Methodist Free Church written by Mr. Edward Plinston. The church had its earliest home in the " old ranters'" chapel in Dallana-lone, which was opened in 1851. Mr. Plinston thus relates the story of its origin : "According to reports of a Conference of the Primitive Methodists I find that in 1850 the Revs. G. Herod and J. Unsworth were stationed in Warrington District (Old-road Chapel). What the methods of conducting the services were at that date, I cannot tell, but the above-mentioned ministers, we are told, cut away the becks of the pews, which caused a split in the congre- gation, one section remaining and the other portion forming a new body—the subject of our record. The founders were William Dutton, William Taylor, Robert Cook, Thomas Gandy, Richard Siddall, John Ashton, H. Ellison, William Richardson, J. Whittle, T. Whittle, and E. Alcock. These few men took the Old Malt Kiln room, in Back Dallam-lane, owned by a widow lady (Mrs. Tinsley, Bewsey-street), at a rental of £lO per year. Then came the task of cleaning and lighting by oil lamps placed against the wall. The opening service was held on the first Sunday in October, 1851, the preacher being William Dutton." ' The progress of the work is described at some length and it is pointed out that the subscribers included : the late Joseph Davies, Robert Davies, Samuel Rigby, George Crostleld, Morland Crosfield,John Crosfleld,John Gordon McMinnies, William Beatnont, Thomas Litton, N. B. Percival, Thomas Morris,Peter Rylands and many others, whose knowledge of the work being done, made them rejoice also for the uplifting of the fallen. The difficulties which were encountered in obtainin,, a new house for the mission on the expiration of the lease of the Dallam building were many but eventually the workers had the satisfaction of securing the plot of land in Buckley-street on which the church and school now stand. The church was opened on April 6th, 1879, I the preachers being Miss Little, of Wigan, morning and ; evening, and the Rev. John Yonge in the afternoon. A meeting to celebrate the opening of the church was held on the following day and the late Mr. John Crosfleltl presided. Buckley-street Mission has been the ceintre of many-sided operations for the uplifting of the people, 'and Mr. Plinston points , out that the school has a fund for feeding the poorest I children in the town during the cold winter months. The school is in a very flourishing condition, in fact more accommodation is needed, and in his concluding sentences Mr. Plinston, in thanking the workers, says : " Some of them have endured the heat and burden of the day for over 50 years, and now they are over 80 , years old say they are anxious to carry home the glad tidings that Buckley-street is free from debt." The Co-operative Hall , has been very attractively decorated for the bazaar and presents a cheerful and inviting appearance. The arrangements have been admirably carried out by a 1 trong committee with Mr.
John Adams as chairman, Mrs.A. Simpson as deputy' chairman. Mr. John Adams as hon.l treasurer, and Messrs J. J. Fairhurst and Ernest A. Sanders as hon. secre- taries.

div.head: , OPEN:NG CEREMONY. Miss Crosfield and the Peace Question.'
div.p: , OPEN:NG CEREMONY. Miss Crosfield and the Peace Question.'

The bazaar was opened on Thursday aftemoon4 Miss Crosfield in the presence of a large gathering. 1 A. H. Crosfield M.P., had been announced to pres but unfortunately indisposition prevented his attek• ance. His place was taken by Mr. James Dodds w, was accompanied by Mrs. Dods. li The CHAIRMAN said he was exceedingly sorry A— he had to stand there in place of their respected meraV ber of Parliament whose health during the recess bad i not been so good as his friends could have wished an°' I consequently he had to cancel all public engagernenta , prior to the meeting of Parliament next week. They all t hoped that he might be fit and well to engage in the work they sent him to do in that assembly ; and that on some occasion ke would come to the Buckley-street friends snd make up for the disappointment of that day. But after 1 ' all they had the presence of Miss Crosfield—(applause) ' and they were proud that she was taking the chief part in that function. He had never seen Miss Crosfield except when she had been engaged in some good work, and he did not think she could put her hand to a better work than she was to undertake that afternoon, t.° 1 further the spiritual and general success of one of thelf ' Christian Churches, He read with great pleasure and interest the admirable history of the origin and progress of the Church, which had heel written by Mr. Edward Plinston, and he could not peruse it without seeingthav the hand and the blessing of God had been on the work. He felt certain that in helping the children' and the children's children of tip saintly founders of that Church' they would be doing god service and helping on the work of God in Use world. (Applause). Miss CROSFIELD, who was heartily received, said she felt very much honoured in being asked to open the " bazaar, for several reasons. The first was that tho. ' saw around them the collective result of a great deal of , self-denying work and spiritual enthusiasm on the part of the workers, and that always commanded her admira- tion. Secondly the mission for which that bazaar N-05 being held had evidently, from its commencement nearly sixty years ago, been like a bright candle shed& lug out its beams in the surrounding gloom. One i had only to read the interesting history of the work la the bazaar handbook to see what help and comfort, radiated from the mission and its workers. They stood' shoulder to shoulder with all those communities which , under differing names and often with differing, opinions on some points, were united for one grand object which they held in common—to help on the good and to beat back the powers of evil. It was veil interesting to read amongst the names of those who helped the work in bye-gone days the names of her father and her uncle. (Applause.) Her brother told her that he was very sorry indeed not tO be present that afternoon. He knew what good work the mission did and he told her to convey his very best wisheS II for the success of the bazaar. He also sent something material to help in what was the more important part of the proceedings, and that. was the spending' (Applause). Miss Crosfield concluded by congratulating the workers on the bright display they had got togeth and, wishing the bazaar all the success which it strongly deserved, she had great pleasure in declaring open. (Applause). - The Rev. J. F. MATTitEwS, in proposing a vote thanks to Miss Crosfield, said that for nearly ten year') he had watched with considerable interest the increas- lug zest of the work carried on in connection with the mission. He knew the stern stress of circumstances associated with the work,how they found it exceedingici difficult to house the children in the Sunday school, how under tremendous odds they were carrying oll,Te services in the church building. Referring pleasure with which they welcomed Miss Crosfield, Matthews said he hoped she would bring her eloqu"' en. to bear in support of the great peace movement, (:),- sociated from military propaganda. He could not hell) but feel that if she went more among the Free Churches . and caught more of their peace-loving spirit, dissom t d from military methods and P an even more useful work among them. (Applause.) d She said that Miss Crosfielcl t Mrs. Dorms seconded. . ropagsnda, she would find took an active part in a great many society functions but she felt sure that there would be no proceedings at which Miss Crosfield might assist, that would give more pleasure to the people that she might be surrounded with than the little function that afternoon. (Applause.) The vote of thanks was passed with enthusiasm. Miss CROSFIELD responded and said she would like Eo tell Mr. Matthews that she was at the present time associated with one of the most active societies for peace that there was in England. It was making for peace, safety, discipline, self-respect and sobriety, strengthening character and conscience and putting awAY y'l Jingoism and hooliganism and everything like that. , She therefore believed that she was-already doing what Mr. Matthews said he hoped she would do. A vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman on the ' proposition of Mr. E. A. SANDERS. • THURSDAY'S PROCEEDS. The proceeds on Thursday amounted to about VO. YESTERDAY'S OPENING. The bazaar was re-opened yesterday afternoon by Mrs Parker, the chair being occupied by Mr. C. E. Parker. Amongst those present were :—Mrs. Garnett, the Rev. J. F. Matthews and Councillor Cunnington. The CHAIR-MAN said he looked upon those small con- gregations of Christian people as centres from which radiated healthy moral Influences which must be for the good of the community. Mr. Parker impressed upon thhi se i rli eoajnerpsarntoictutlaorcnoenifignhebotuherbmosoedlvbeustttoothreeaelffi zoer ttshaint there was a great stream of life as yet untouched bY the Churches. He hoped that some day it might be possible in towns like Warrington for the Free Churches to unite not only to hold open-air services but to have a united Free Church permanent mission. (Applause). Mrs. PARKER delivered a neat speeeh in which she Said the work at Buckley-street was one of high effort and strenuous life among people well worthy of help and who needed it most. (Applause). On the motion of ConneillOr CUNNINGTON, seconded by the Rev. J. F. MATTHEWS, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs. Parker. THE ENTERTAINMENTS. An excellent series of side-shows and entertainments has been well patronized. Numerous amusing competi- tions have been watched with interest and visitors have tried their luck at the fishing well and bran tub. Another popular feature is an exhibition of living wax- works. At intervals miscellaneous concerts have been given, the artistes being : —The Apollo Male Quartet, Messrs. %V. Critchley, R. Cook, W. Woodcock, D. Gittens; sopranos, Miss Jenny Jones (St.Helens), Miss Sumner, Mrs. J. Randall, Miss Alice Woodland ; contraltos, Miss Line Plinston and Miss Lily Fairhurst; tenors, Mr. Charles Fairhurst, Mr. W. Critchley, Mr. R. Cook ; baritone, Mr. D. Gittens ; bass Mr. W Woodcock ; solo oboe, Mr. G. Clarke ; 'duets, The Misses Woodland and Fairhurst, Miss Fairhurst and Mr. Chafles Fairhurst ; duets (piano), Miss Edith Blake and Miss Ivy Rigby: humorist, Mr. Arthur Maybury ; •" accompanist, Miss H. Plinston, A.L.C.M. ' Selections have been given by an orchestra under the 1 conductorship of Mr. H. A. Roberts, and concerts by the St. Clement's Minstrel Troupe have proved popular. To-day (Saturday) there will be an exhibition of fancy ' ' glass blowing by Mr. %V. Langley, of St. Helens. There is a comfortable smoke-room and lounge under . the management of Messrs. T. COUNTY BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. MUNICIPAL BLBOTIONS, 1935. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE LATCHFORD WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— I have consented tta be nominated for your representatlion. For four or five years I havf taken a prominen t part in the most important mora7 movement which has been seers in Warrington amok its incor poratio n—the strenuous and costly struggle for civi c purity. At sixteen great public meetings in the Parr Hall and at contested elections in every ward but one, the ratepayera have endorsed the plctform of the reformers. Sound public policy has always dictated that there should be no personal interest accruing to nubile repre- rentatives as the result of their membership of public bodies. i. The present Government and the House of Commons, In reference to the conduct of their respective members, are scrupulously exacting in this regard ; your present Member of Parliament and your late Conservative Member in January last clearly and categorically approved the principle that tt no representative elected to any public body should derive pecuniary profit or pay- ment, directly or indirectly,by reason of his membership of such body." The Municipal Corporations Acts specifically enact that trading, or the receiving of profit by members of Corporations, renders such members ineligible to hold office. Of the seven years covered by the late Trading Inquiry, Alderman Bennett held the office of Mayor's auditor for five years and received £l5O, and for the last two years of the per led Mr. A. J. Jolley held the position and received £6O. The Non-Traders challenged these payments as clearly illegal and the electors of Fairfield Ward, in November 1902, rejected Mr. A, J. Yolley, who at the time of his defeat was acting as the Mayor's Auditor, by the enormous majority of 790 votes Since that memorable election no one has accepted any fee as Mayor's Auditor until this year. Mr. W. J. Wilson, the retiring candidate for your Ward, having sought oat and informed Councillors Pemberton and Lord that-he would not take any payment, acceded the office and, a few weeks ago, contrary to his own clear declaration, received from the Borough Treasurer £3O as payment for his services. This payment being, as I believed, highly improper as well as illegal. I immediately announced through the press that the moral issues involved would have to be fought out at the forthcoming election. In pursu- ance of that announcement a candidate was at once selected who owing to imperative medical advice, has bad to abandon his candidature and, in the abaence of any other substitute, I have no alternative but to take his place, The supreme issues upon which I desire your Verdict are (1) Whether Councillor Wilson can henceforth act as an independent, representative of the ratepayers ; whether he has not in short male himself a mere pawn or tool of the party from whom he has receiVed the office which has yielded him the £3) he has received, and whether. if so. he is a fit and proper representative for your Ward. (2) Whether you are not satisfied that the chief " evils which have disgraced our Municipal government In Warrington have arisen from and are the inevitcbie result of the mixing up of the affairs of the town with the party politics of the nation, and of the State ; that the lines upon which national parties divide have no necessary count ction with the business of a town " ; and that !such connection opens the way for political com- pacts, and behind these " for countless schemes of public plunder and civic corruption." And if so (3) Whether It is not time that you ceased electing representatives for purely business duties merely because they are Conservative or Liberal, or blue or red. The issue, ladies and gentlemen, is in your hands. I have not sottght nor do I covet election. I shall not persostally canvass a single burgess, but if you approve my past and present public wor tr,if you think I can serve you, I will undertak if you vote for me. and I should be returned, to do what I can, with a single eye to your best interests and Your faith: ul service. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient servant, JAMBS DODDS. October Mb. 1003.

COUNTY BOROUGH OF WattRING VON. UNIC 1 PAL EL ECTIO No 1906.—T0 THE ELECTORS OF ST. JOHN'S WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, Three years ago, by the largest majority ever given to A municipal candidate in Warrington. you did me the honour to send me to the Town Council AS your indepen- dent representative, and I shall again ask you on November Ist for a renewal of yle confidence you reposed in me in 1903. I again have the honour of offering myself as an inde- pendent candidate in the interests of the general body of ratepayers and residents in your ward. I am not the nominee of any party, political, relig'ous, or social, believing as I do, that to serve the best interests of ars town is the only true and proper object to be aimed at. I am not connected with any clique or faction, nor will I do the bidding of any body of People, but the electors themselves pifdze myself to any plitlcal or religions body, as faussi to cannot ewe the advantage of Parr saint og into the management of 'octil concerns any particular it of views appertaining to Imperial or Parliamentary politics. Whatever MY view. may be on Imperial affairs. I own no allegiance to any party or RI oup of persons, and I hold mybelf perfectly free in the future, ass t have always done In the past, to support any gclori movement that may be brought forward for the gefteral welfare of the town. Of course, I do not claim it as my own work alone, but you can easily see a great change for the better has bk en bronght about in the ward within the last three years. Your streets and back pasiages are better paved and in a more healthy condition. Your street lighting Is much improved. There are more recreation grounds for your little ones in the district. There is a more efficient and cheaper tram service in the town than formerly The tramways are now makings profit and helping the rates, whereas they were previously making a loss. The price of gas has been reduced to the slot meter users a. well aa to the more wealthy ratepayers. Notwithstanding all this, there has been a consider- able reduction in the rates dosing the past year, but Share still remains ft great deal to be altered and improved in the town, more pard.wlarly in St. John's Ward. I am, and have always been a strong advocate for a tram or motor bus service through Orford Lane and Bittersby Lane before any more favours are granted to those well provided districts which have these great facilities at the present time. Also, there still remains, I regret to say, a great deal of unsanitary and uninhabitable property In your ward, which should be made more suitable for human hatt a- lion. or else condemoed altogether, and this I hope wilt be brought about in the near future. I shall continue to press for the erection of a bridge across the river from Howley into Victoria ?ark in order to open up direct communication between Latchford and your ward and neighbourhood, and also to develop Victoria Park by letting it out in allotments for the benefit of the people, or by any other suitable scheme, whereby it would be made a sconce of profit for the com- munity instead of it being a dead loss as it is at the present time. In conclusion, ladles and gentlemen, It you do me the honour of re-electing me as one of your representatives, I will do all I can for your ward and the town in general and will not be subject to the command of any party but the ratepayers. themselves, and I feel confident that the time has come when your experience and intelligence have taught you that the only suitable person to repre- sent 3ou is one absolutely independent of all political parties and whose Interests are identical with your own. My record for the past three years is before you ell. I ask yoit by your votes on November Ist to say that in what I have done, and tried to do for the ward and town generally, I have your hearty approval. am. Indies and Gentlemen, Your humble servant to command, JOHN aIaGINN.

No Friend like a Sister.—Once again this autumn Miss Rosa Nouchette Carey has given us a delightful book, and in so far as she introduces her readers to a charming family of three eaters and a brother, her latest work resembles that of a year ago, viz., "The Household of Peter." The amendment was then withdrawn and the decisions of the committee with the addition named by Mr. Linaker were approved. <421. EVENING CONTINUATION CLASSES. Distribution of Prizes. The prizes won in connection with the Evening Continuation School at People's College, were distributed on Tuesday evening in the presence of a large attendance of students. Mr. JOHN UPSON who presided referred to the facili- ties which the Education Committee offered to boys and girls to gain knowledge and if any youth or maiden did not avail himself or herself of the facilities then the fault lay with them. So far thecommittee had not been disappointed. The students should not rest con- tent with merely passing through the branch technical school. They should go on until they had exhausted every provision which the committee had made for their mental training. Alderman BENNETT, chairman of the Education Com- mittee, in distributing the prizes, said the work of the past aession at that evening school—judging by the results of the Union of Lancashire and Cheshire Institutes—showed a considerable improvement in quality on that of previous years. Twenty-one passed in the intermediate stage and 81 in the elementary, the total percentage of successes being 84. One pleasing feature was the remarkable success of the girls in cookery, domestic economy, and needlework. All their students passed in cookery and needlework, and only one failed in domestic economy, while one obtained fourth place in the Union of Lancashire and Cheshire Institutes, and so gained distinction. They had every reason to be proud of their record, and proud of the school. PRIZE LIST. The following were the prize-winners : DOTS.
